query.original_query: sparse autoencoder features encode quantitative magnitude vs categorical concepts in language models numerical dosage

sub_queries.semantic_query: sparse autoencoder features encoding quantitative magnitude versus categorical concepts in language models, numerical dosage representation, feature dictionary learning for continuous features
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how sparse autoencoders trained on language model activations represent continuous quantitative magnitudes, such as numerical dosages, compared to categorical concepts. Using dictionary learning applied to the residual stream, we analyze feature activations across scalar quantities and discrete categories. Our analysis reveals that features encoding numerical values often exhibit graded activation patterns proportional to magnitude, contrasting with the binary activation typical of categorical features. We find that these continuous features are less polysemantic than those encoding categorical concepts, yet they are more prone to feature splitting, where distinct features activate for different ranges of the same quantity. Reconstruction fidelity for quantitative inputs is higher when the autoencoder allocates multiple features to cover the magnitude spectrum, suggesting a trade-off between L0 sparsity and representational granularity. Results show that dead features are less common for continuous features, but feature absorption—where a single feature dominates multiple related magnitudes—can obscure fine-grained distinctions. Our findings highlight challenges in sparse feature decomposition for continuous variables, with implications for interpretability and feature steering in numerical reasoning tasks.

sub_queries.semantic_query: sparse autoencoder features encode quantitative magnitude vs categorical concepts in language models numerical dosage
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) features in large language models encode quantitative magnitude as a continuous variable or as discrete categorical concepts, using numerical dosage as a test case. We extracted SAE features from intermediate layers of a transformer-based language model and measured their activation patterns across sentences describing varying dosages (e.g., "5 mg", "50 mg", "500 mg"). Using linear probing and representational similarity analysis, we compared the geometry of feature representations to both a continuous numerical scale and a set of categorical bins (low, medium, high). Results indicate that SAE features predominantly encode dosage as a categorical concept rather than a continuous magnitude, with distinct feature clusters corresponding to discrete ranges. However, a subset of features exhibited monotonic activation scaling consistent with a continuous encoding. Findings support the hypothesis that sparse autoencoder representations in language models capture both categorical and graded quantitative information, with categorical encoding dominating for numerical dosage. These results have implications for interpretability research and the reliability of numerical reasoning in large language models.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: k-Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How effective is sparsity by itself as a regularizer and nonlinearity in autoencoders for feature learning and classification?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the k-sparse autoencoder, a fast sparse coding method that enforces exact sparsity in hidden units, and shows it achieves better classification results than denoising autoencoders, dropout, and RBMs on MNIST and NORB.
papers.conclusion: The k-sparse autoencoder is a fast and effective sparse coding method that achieves state-of-the-art classification results by enforcing sparsity alone, without other nonlinearities or penalties.
papers.key_findings:
The k-sparse autoencoder achieves better classification performance than denoising autoencoders, dropout autoencoders, and RBMs on MNIST and NORB datasets.
The sparsity level k controls the locality of learned features; higher k yields more local features, lower k yields more global features.
The method is simple to train and fast for encoding, making it suitable for large problem sizes.
k-sparse autoencoders can be used for pre-training shallow and deep discriminative neural networks, achieving results comparable to state-of-the-art.
A scheduling strategy for the sparsity level during training helps avoid dead hidden units and improves training.
papers.limitation: Too low sparsity level (k) can lead to dead hidden units and features that are too global, not factoring the input into parts.
papers.abstract: Recently, it has been observed that when representations are learnt in a way that encourages sparsity, improved performance is obtained on classification tasks. These methods involve combinations of activation functions, sampling steps and different kinds of penalties. To investigate the effectiveness of sparsity by itself, we propose the k-sparse autoencoder, which is an autoencoder with linear activation function, where in hidden layers only the k highest activities are kept. When applied to the MNIST and NORB datasets, we find that this method achieves better classification results than denoising autoencoders, networks trained with dropout, and RBMs. k-sparse autoencoders are simple to train and the encoding stage is very fast, making them well-suited to large problem sizes, where conventional sparse coding algorithms cannot be applied.

papers.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What causes Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to fail in recovering true underlying features when the features form a hierarchy? The paper identifies and studies the phenomenon of feature absorption.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of feature absorption in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), showing it is caused by hierarchical features and the sparsity penalty, and introduces a metric to detect it.
papers.conclusion: Feature absorption poses an obstacle to the practical application of SAEs for interpretability, and fundamental theoretical issues need to be addressed before SAEs can be used robustly at scale.
papers.key_findings:
Feature absorption occurs in SAEs when features form a hierarchy, causing seemingly monosemantic latents to fail to fire where they should.
The phenomenon is caused by the sparsity penalty in SAEs.
The paper proposes a metric to detect feature absorption and validates it on hundreds of LLM SAEs.
Feature absorption is widespread and occurs in every LLM SAE tested.
Varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve the issue.
papers.limitation:
The absorption metric is limited to early layers (before layer 18 in Gemma 2 2B) because attention moves information to later tokens, making causal interventions ineffective at later layers.
The absorption metric is likely an underestimate of true absorption because it only captures cases where a single latent dominates and the main latents are fully turned off.
future_direction: Develop improved metrics for feature absorption that can be applied at all model layers and capture partial absorption.
Address the fundamental theoretical issues causing feature absorption to enable robust use of SAEs for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) aim to decompose the activation space of large language models (LLMs) into human-interpretable latent directions or features. As we increase the number of features in the SAE, hierarchical features tend to split into finer features ("math" may split into "algebra", "geometry", etc.), a phenomenon referred to as feature splitting. However, we show that sparse decomposition and splitting of hierarchical features is not robust. Specifically, we show that seemingly monosemantic features fail to fire where they should, and instead get "absorbed" into their children features. We coin this phenomenon feature absorption, and show that it is caused by optimizing for sparsity in SAEs whenever the underlying features form a hierarchy. We introduce a metric to detect absorption in SAEs, and validate our findings empirically on hundreds of LLM SAEs. Our investigation suggests that varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve this issue. We discuss the implications of feature absorption in SAEs and some potential approaches to solve the fundamental theoretical issues before SAEs can be used for interpreting LLMs robustly and at scale.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
papers.research_question: How do concept activation distributions differ between Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and their base models, and do SAEs promote more monosemantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a distribution-aware concept separability score and shows that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability than their dense base models. It also proposes a new intervention method, Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), which enables effective concept removal with minimal side effects.
papers.conclusion: This work presents the first quantitative analysis of monosemanticity in SAEs compared to dense base models through a distributional lens, introduces a fine-grained concept separability score, and proposes a new intervention method (APP) that achieves effective concept removal with the least possible side effects.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit lower polysemanticity (neuron overlap) and higher concept separability than their base models across multiple datasets and models.
SAEs enable more precise concept-level interventions than base models, particularly when using partial suppression methods.
The proposed APP intervention method achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly competitive at concept removal.
Higher-capacity SAEs (e.g., 65k dimensions) yield greater concept separability and more effective interventions than lower-capacity ones.
A strong positive correlation exists between the concept separability score and the precision of partial concept erasure methods.
papers.limitation: APP uses a histogram-based approximation for density estimation to improve computational efficiency, which trades off accuracy and computational cost. Achieving the best possible performance requires significantly higher computational resources.
future_direction: Future work could explore alternative kernel density estimation (KDE) methods to better balance accuracy and efficiency for the APP method.
papers.abstract: A key barrier to interpreting large language models is polysemanticity, where neurons activate for multiple unrelated concepts. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed to mitigate this issue by transforming dense activations into sparse, more interpretable features. While prior work suggests that SAEs promote monosemanticity, no quantitative comparison has examined how concept activation distributions differ between SAEs and their base models. This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of SAEs against base models through activation distribution lens. We introduce a fine-grained concept separability score based on the Jensen-Shannon distance, which captures how distinctly a neuron's activation distributions vary across concepts. Using two large language models (Gemma-2-2B and DeepSeek-R1) and multiple SAE variants across five datasets (including word-level and sentence-level), we show that SAEs reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability. To assess practical utility, we evaluate concept-level interventions using two strategies: full neuron masking and partial suppression. We find that, compared to base models, SAEs enable more precise concept-level control when using partial suppression. Building on this, we propose Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), a new intervention method that uses concept-conditioned activation distributions for targeted suppression. APP achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly effective at concept removal.

papers.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scale sparse autoencoders to large language models and how should we evaluate their quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for scaling sparse autoencoders using a TopK activation function to directly control sparsity and techniques to prevent dead latents, establishes scaling laws, and proposes new metrics for evaluating feature quality.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can be scaled effectively with the proposed methods, and larger autoencoders yield better features according to the introduced evaluation metrics.
papers.key_findings:
TopK activation function improves the reconstruction-sparsity frontier and simplifies training compared to ReLU autoencoders with L1 penalty.
Techniques like tied initialization and an auxiliary loss reduce dead latents to 7% in a 16 million latent autoencoder.
Clean scaling laws are found with respect to autoencoder size and sparsity.
Larger autoencoders generally improve feature quality according to new metrics (probe loss, explainability, ablation sparsity).
The method scales to training a 16 million latent autoencoder on GPT-4 activations.
papers.limitation:
The probe-based evaluation metric leans on strong assumptions about what kinds of features are natural.
Evaluating explanation precision for arbitrary English explanations is computationally expensive.
future_direction: Explore ways to make it more tractable to approximate precision for arbitrary English explanations.
Scale to even larger autoencoders and apply the method to other models and modalities.
Improve evaluation metrics for feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders provide a promising unsupervised approach for extracting interpretable features from a language model by reconstructing activations from a sparse bottleneck layer. Since language models learn many concepts, autoencoders need to be very large to recover all relevant features. However, studying the properties of autoencoder scaling is difficult due to the need to balance reconstruction and sparsity objectives and the presence of dead latents. We propose using k-sparse autoencoders [Makhzani and Frey, 2013] to directly control sparsity, simplifying tuning and improving the reconstruction-sparsity frontier. Additionally, we find modifications that result in few dead latents, even at the largest scales we tried. Using these techniques, we find clean scaling laws with respect to autoencoder size and sparsity. We also introduce several new metrics for evaluating feature quality based on the recovery of hypothesized features, the explainability of activation patterns, and the sparsity of downstream effects. These metrics all generally improve with autoencoder size. To demonstrate the scalability of our approach, we train a 16 million latent autoencoder on GPT-4 activations for 40 billion tokens. We release training code and autoencoders for open-source models, as well as a visualizer.

papers.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable monosemantic features from polysemantic activations in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes PS-Eval, a new evaluation metric and dataset for assessing whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations. It finds that SAEs optimized for MSE-L0 Pareto frontier do not necessarily improve monosemantic feature extraction, and that deeper layers and attention mechanisms contribute to distinguishing polysemous words.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes Poly-Semantic Evaluation (PS-Eval), a new metric and dataset to assess the ability of SAEs to extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations, in complement to traditional MSE or L0 metrics. The work encourages the community to conduct holistic evaluations of SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability and do not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features.
Deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word.
Increasing the latent dimension of SAEs generally improves specificity up to a saturation point.
Activation functions like TopK and JumpReLU, designed to improve MSE-L0 trade-off, do not perform well on PS-Eval metrics; ReLU performs best.
SAE features are more interpretable than raw LLM activations for polysemous words.
papers.limitation: PS-Eval relies on evaluating the maximum activation of SAE features, which may not always align with intended word meanings and could introduce ambiguity.
future_direction: Incorporate similarity metrics that utilize the distribution of SAE features, rather than relying solely on maximum activation.
Extend PS-Eval beyond natural language to other domains such as diffusion models and vision-language models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have gained a lot of attention as a promising tool to improve the interpretability of large language models (LLMs) by mapping the complex superposition of polysemantic neurons into monosemantic features and composing a sparse dictionary of words. However, traditional performance metrics like Mean Squared Error and L0 sparsity ignore the evaluation of the semantic representational power of SAEs -- whether they can acquire interpretable monosemantic features while preserving the semantic relationship of words. For instance, it is not obvious whether a learned sparse feature could distinguish different meanings in one word. In this paper, we propose a suite of evaluations for SAEs to analyze the quality of monosemantic features by focusing on polysemous words. Our findings reveal that SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability, which does not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features. The analysis of SAEs with polysemous words can also figure out the internal mechanism of LLMs; deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word. Our semantics focused evaluation offers new insights into the polysemy and the existing SAE objective and contributes to the development of more practical SAEs.

papers.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders extract relatively monosemantic features that are more interpretable than neurons, with most features being human-understandable.
Features can be used to intervene on and steer transformer generation, such as activating specific features to produce corresponding text like base64 or Arabic script.
Features are universal across different models and autoencoder runs, more similar to each other than to neurons, suggesting they reflect underlying data properties.
Features split into families as autoencoder size increases, providing different resolutions of understanding the same model components.
Despite having only 512 neurons, the MLP layer can represent tens of thousands of features through superposition, as shown by scaling the autoencoder.
papers.abstract: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition? Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis. Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Empirical Evaluation of Progressive Coding for Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently obtain high-fidelity, interpretable SAEs of different sizes for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces and compares two methods for progressive coding in sparse autoencoders (Matryoshka SAEs and a permutation/pruning method), demonstrating a trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper discusses the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and interpretability in progressive SAE methods, suggesting that Matryoshka SAEs offer better performance while pruned SAEs offer better interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary importance in vanilla SAEs follows a power law.
Matryoshka SAEs exhibit lower reconstruction loss and higher representational similarity compared to baseline SAEs.
Pruned vanilla SAEs (via permutation) are more interpretable than Matryoshka SAEs.
Both methods allow efficient progressive coding, with Matryoshka SAEs performing better on reconstruction fidelity.
Feature splitting occurs as SAE size increases, affecting performance when using only a subset of features.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively modest-sized SAEs compared to recent work, and methods remain to be validated at larger scales.
Decoder kernel implementation leads to redundant computations in Matryoshka SAEs.
Feature-splitting presents a limitation when distilling large SAEs into smaller ones via permutation, as selecting only the most important split features fails to capture complete functionality.
future_direction: Validating methods at larger scales.
Improving decoder kernel implementation to avoid redundant computations.
Developing methods to recombine or reverse feature-splitting during distillation.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) \citep{bricken2023monosemanticity,gao2024scalingevaluatingsparseautoencoders} rely on dictionary learning to extract interpretable features from neural networks at scale in an unsupervised manner, with applications to representation engineering and information retrieval. SAEs are, however, computationally expensive \citep{lieberum2024gemmascopeopensparse}, especially when multiple SAEs of different sizes are needed. We show that dictionary importance in vanilla SAEs follows a power law. We compare progressive coding based on subset pruning of SAEs -- to jointly training nested SAEs, or so-called {\em Matryoshka} SAEs \citep{bussmann2024learning,nabeshima2024Matryoshka} -- on a language modeling task. We show Matryoshka SAEs exhibit lower reconstruction loss and recaptured language modeling loss, as well as higher representational similarity. Pruned vanilla SAEs are more interpretable, however. We discuss the origins and implications of this trade-off.

papers.title: The Geometry of Concepts: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Structure
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of sparse autoencoder features at atomic, intermediate, and large scales?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features exhibit geometric structure at three scales: atomic crystal structures (parallelograms/trapezoids), intermediate functional lobes (e.g., for math and code), and large-scale anisotropic point clouds with power-law eigenvalue spectra.
papers.conclusion: SAE features have geometric structure at multiple scales, which may help understand how networks represent features and improve AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Atomic-scale crystal structures (parallelograms/trapezoids) are revealed after projecting out distractor features using linear discriminant analysis (LDA).
Intermediate-scale functional lobes exist where co-occurring features (e.g., math and code features) cluster together spatially, quantified by mutual information and classification accuracy.
Large-scale point cloud structure is anisotropic with a power-law eigenvalue spectrum, steepest in middle layers.
Clustering entropy (negentropy) is lower in middle layers, indicating more structured representations.
The eigenvalue spectrum of SAE features decays as a power law, more steeply than for raw activations.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain why the observed geometric structure forms.
future_direction: Further work to explain the origin of the geometric structure in SAE features.
Investigate whether variations in structure across layers depend on the prominence of crystals or lobes or have a different origin.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders have recently produced dictionaries of high-dimensional vectors corresponding to the universe of concepts represented by large language models. We find that this concept universe has interesting structure at three levels: 1) The "atomic" small-scale structure contains "crystals" whose faces are parallelograms or trapezoids, generalizing well-known examples such as (man-woman-king-queen). We find that the quality of such parallelograms and associated function vectors improves greatly when projecting out global distractor directions such as word length, which is efficiently done with linear discriminant analysis. 2) The "brain" intermediate-scale structure has significant spatial modularity; for example, math and code features form a "lobe" akin to functional lobes seen in neural fMRI images. We quantify the spatial locality of these lobes with multiple metrics and find that clusters of co-occurring features, at coarse enough scale, also cluster together spatially far more than one would expect if feature geometry were random. 3) The "galaxy" scale large-scale structure of the feature point cloud is not isotropic, but instead has a power law of eigenvalues with steepest slope in middle layers. We also quantify how the clustering entropy depends on the layer.

papers.title: From Atoms to Trees: Building a Structured Feature Forest with Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to capture the hierarchical structure of features in LLM representations, moving beyond isolated feature extraction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (HSAE), a method that jointly learns sparse autoencoders and parent-child relationships to extract hierarchical feature structures from LLM representations.
papers.conclusion: HSAE is a novel framework that learns conceptual hierarchies from LLM activations, outperforming post-hoc methods and preserving SAE feature quality.
papers.key_findings:
HSAE recovers semantically meaningful hierarchies from LLM activations, as shown by qualitative case studies and quantitative metrics.
HSAE significantly outperforms post-hoc alignment baselines in hierarchical consistency (e.g., lower Hamming distance, higher co-activation probabilities).
HSAE maintains feature quality and reconstruction fidelity comparable to standard SAEs across various dictionary sizes.
The learned hierarchies manifest geometrically: activations triggering sibling features cluster together in the activation space.
Features with multiple children exhibit higher interpretability (AutoInterp scores) than those with a single child.
papers.limitation:
The tree structure is constrained by a fixed number of levels, which may not fully capture varying depths of semantic abstraction.
Some misalignments in parent-child co-activation persist, and it is unclear if they are due to methodological constraints or inherently non-hierarchical activations.
future_direction: Investigate more flexible architectural priors and scaling laws of hierarchical discovery.
Apply hierarchies for multi-scale model steering and safety auditing.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven effective for extracting monosemantic features from large language models (LLMs), yet these features are typically identified in isolation. However, broad evidence suggests that LLMs capture the intrinsic structure of natural language, where the phenomenon of "feature splitting" in particular indicates that such structure is hierarchical. To capture this, we propose the Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (HSAE), which jointly learns a series of SAEs and the parent-child relationships between their features. HSAE strengthens the alignment between parent and child features through two novel mechanisms: a structural constraint loss and a random feature perturbation mechanism. Extensive experiments across various LLMs and layers demonstrate that HSAE consistently recovers semantically meaningful hierarchies, supported by both qualitative case studies and rigorous quantitative metrics. At the same time, HSAE preserves the reconstruction fidelity and interpretability of standard SAEs across different dictionary sizes. Our work provides a powerful, scalable tool for discovering and analyzing the multi-scale conceptual structures embedded in LLM representations.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Trained on the Same Data Learn Different Features
papers.research_question: Does the random seed used to initialize sparse autoencoders affect the features they learn when trained on the same data and model?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs trained on the same data and model with different random seeds learn different features, suggesting that SAE features are not universal but rather pragmatic decompositions of activation space.
papers.conclusion: SAEs do not uncover a universal set of features; feature discovery should be viewed as a compositional, hierarchical problem due to the nonconvexity of the loss function.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained with different random seeds identify different sets of features, with only 30% shared in Llama 3 8B.
Shared features tend to fire more frequently and are more interpretable than orphan features.
Orphan features can still be interpretable, indicating that individual SAE runs may miss interpretable features.
Feature overlap decreases with more SAE latents and increases with longer training time.
ReLU SAEs with L1 loss show greater stability across seeds compared to TopK SAEs.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a useful tool for uncovering human-interpretable features in the activations of large language models (LLMs). While some expect SAEs to find the true underlying features used by a model, our research shows that SAEs trained on the same model and data, differing only in the random seed used to initialize their weights, identify different sets of features. For example, in an SAE with 131K latents trained on a feedforward network in Llama 3 8B, only 30% of the features were shared across different seeds. We observed this phenomenon across multiple layers of three different LLMs, two datasets, and several SAE architectures. While ReLU SAEs trained with the L1 sparsity loss showed greater stability across seeds, SAEs using the state-of-the-art TopK activation function were more seed-dependent, even when controlling for the level of sparsity. Our results suggest that the set of features uncovered by an SAE should be viewed as a pragmatically useful decomposition of activation space, rather than an exhaustive and universal list of features "truly used" by the model.

papers.title: Temporal Sparse Autoencoders: Leveraging the Sequential Nature of Language for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate temporal consistency into sparse autoencoders to better recover high-level semantic features in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs) that incorporate a temporal contrastive loss to encourage consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens, leading to better disentanglement of semantic and syntactic features in language models.
papers.conclusion: Temporal SAEs leverage the sequential nature of language to better extract semantic features, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.
papers.key_findings:
T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
T-SAEs exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal.
T-SAEs show improved disentanglement between high-level (semantic) and low-level (syntactic) features.
T-SAEs provide practical interpretability benefits, such as in safety monitoring and steering.
papers.abstract: Translating the internal representations and computations of models into concepts that humans can understand is a key goal of interpretability. While recent dictionary learning methods such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising route to discover human-interpretable features, they suffer from a variety of problems, including a systematic failure to capture the rich conceptual information that drives linguistic understanding. Instead, they exhibit a bias towards shallow, token-specific, or noisy features, such as "the phrase 'The' at the start of sentences". In this work, we propose that this is due to a fundamental issue with how dictionary learning methods for LLMs are trained. Language itself has a rich, well-studied structure spanning syntax, semantics, and pragmatics; however, current unsupervised methods largely ignore this linguistic knowledge, leading to poor feature discovery that favors superficial patterns over meaningful concepts. We focus on a simple but important aspect of language: semantic content has long-range dependencies and tends to be smooth over a sequence, whereas syntactic information is much more local. Building on this insight, we introduce Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs), which incorporate a novel contrastive loss encouraging consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens. This simple yet powerful modification enables SAEs to disentangle semantic from syntactic features in a self-supervised manner. Across multiple datasets and models, T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality. Strikingly, they exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.

papers.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
papers.research_question: Does incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improve the reconstruction-interpretability frontier? Specifically, does it improve reconstruction, maintain or improve interpretability, and learn hierarchical semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (H-SAE) architecture that explicitly models semantic hierarchy, improving reconstruction performance and interpretability while being computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improves the reconstruction-interpretability frontier, leading to better reconstruction, maintained or improved interpretability, and learned hierarchical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
H-SAEs have better reconstruction performance than standard SAEs as measured by explained variance and downstream CE loss.
H-SAEs maintain or improve interpretability, showing less feature absorption and fewer redundant features across languages.
The H-SAE architecture learns hierarchical semantics, with high-level features capturing general concepts and low-level features capturing specific instances.
The hierarchical structure provides significant computational efficiency gains, allowing scaling to larger effective dictionary sizes with minimal overhead.
The architecture successfully translates theoretical insights about hierarchical concept geometry into a practical mixture-of-experts type model.
papers.limitation: Results are still imperfect, with some hard-to-interpret features and far from perfect reconstruction.
future_direction: Explore other reconstruction objectives beyond Euclidean distance.
Incorporate insights from causal representation learning into LLM interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (and, in particular, sparse autoencoders) attempts to learn a set of human-understandable concepts that can explain variation on an abstract space. A basic limitation of this approach is that it neither exploits nor represents the semantic relationships between the learned concepts. In this paper, we introduce a modified SAE architecture that explicitly models a semantic hierarchy of concepts. Application of this architecture to the internal representations of large language models shows both that semantic hierarchy can be learned, and that doing so improves both reconstruction and interpretability. Additionally, the architecture leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency.

papers.title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the amortisation gap in sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and can more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that sparse autoencoder (SAE) encoders are inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference due to an amortisation gap, and demonstrates empirically that more expressive encoders (like MLPs) and sparse coding methods can outperform SAEs, leading to more interpretable features in large language models.
papers.conclusion: More sophisticated sparse inference methods, such as MLPs and sparse coding, can outperform traditional SAE encoders, reducing the amortisation gap and improving interpretability, which opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAE encoders have a provable amortisation gap, making them suboptimal for sparse inference even in solvable cases.
Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and sparse coding consistently outperform SAEs in recovering sparse codes, with sparse coding achieving the highest performance.
The performance advantage of more sophisticated methods is more pronounced in regimes where compressed sensing theory predicts recoverability.
These findings generalize to real-world applications, as shown by training on GPT-2 activations where MLPs yield more interpretable features than SAEs.
The amortisation gap can be reduced with increased compute, with MLPs surpassing SAE performance after a consistent computational threshold.
papers.limitation: The theoretical result on SAE suboptimality is proven for a specific setting (linear-nonlinear encoder, sparse signals in union of subspaces) and may not cover all practical SAE implementations.
future_direction: Pitting optimised sparse coding approaches (e.g., Least Angle Regression, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit) against optimised SAE architectures.
Further exploration of top-k sparse coding with proper hyperparameter tuning to achieve Pareto improvements.
Scaling the methods to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: A recent line of work has shown promise in using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to uncover interpretable features in neural network representations. However, the simple linear-nonlinear encoding mechanism in SAEs limits their ability to perform accurate sparse inference. Using compressed sensing theory, we prove that an SAE encoder is inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference, even in solvable cases. We then decouple encoding and decoding processes to empirically explore conditions where more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders. Our results reveal substantial performance gains with minimal compute increases in correct inference of sparse codes. We demonstrate this generalises to SAEs applied to large language models, where more expressive encoders achieve greater interpretability. This work opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations and analysing large language model activations.

papers.title: Taming Polysemanticity in LLMs: Provable Feature Recovery via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to formulate a statistical model for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations, and design an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and practical effectiveness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a statistical framework for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations and proposes Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and improved empirical performance.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a statistical framework and the GBA algorithm for provable feature recovery in SAEs, advancing mechanistic interpretability with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Proposes a statistical model that formalizes polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts.
Introduces Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm that uses bias adaptation to control neuron sparsity without hyperparameter tuning.
Provides the first provable recovery guarantee for an SAE algorithm, showing GBA recovers all monosemantic features under the statistical model.
Empirically demonstrates GBA achieves superior sparsity-loss trade-off and feature consistency on LLMs up to 1.5B parameters compared to baseline methods.
future_direction: Extending the statistical framework to more complex data distributions.
Scaling GBA to larger models.
Exploring applications in model steering and control.
papers.abstract: We study the challenge of achieving theoretically grounded feature recovery using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for the interpretation of Large Language Models. Existing SAE training algorithms often lack rigorous mathematical guarantees and suffer from practical limitations such as hyperparameter sensitivity and instability. To address these issues, we first propose a novel statistical framework for the feature recovery problem, which includes a new notion of feature identifiability by modeling polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts. Building on this framework, we introduce a new SAE training algorithm based on ``bias adaptation'', a technique that adaptively adjusts neural network bias parameters to ensure appropriate activation sparsity. We theoretically \highlight{prove that this algorithm correctly recovers all monosemantic features} when input data is sampled from our proposed statistical model. Furthermore, we develop an improved empirical variant, Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), and \highlight{demonstrate its superior performance against benchmark methods when applied to LLMs with up to 1.5 billion parameters}. This work represents a foundational step in demystifying SAE training by providing the first SAE algorithm with theoretical recovery guarantees, thereby advancing the development of more transparent and trustworthy AI systems through enhanced mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: AbsTopK: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders For Bidirectional Features
papers.research_question: Is the use of nonnegative activations truly essential for the success of SAEs, or does it constrain their ability to capture richer representations? Can SAEs be improved by allowing negative activations, enabling the discovery of bidirectional concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AbsTopK SAE, a sparse autoencoder variant that removes the non-negativity constraint, enabling single latent features to encode bidirectional semantic concepts and improving reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Removing the non-negativity constraint in SAEs via the AbsTopK operator allows single features to capture bipolar semantics and yields reconstructions of superior compactness and fidelity, pioneering a shift towards bipolar sparse representations.
papers.key_findings:
AbsTopK SAE enables single latent features to encode opposing concepts by leveraging both positive and negative activations.
AbsTopK outperforms TopK and JumpReLU SAEs in reconstruction fidelity and interpretability across multiple models and tasks.
AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the supervised Difference-in-Mean method on some steering tasks.
The non-negativity constraint in existing SAEs fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness.
AbsTopK achieves a better balance between safety alignment (HarmBench) and general capability preservation (MMLU) compared to conventional SAE steering.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-step variants, yielding multi-layer encoders that produce more accurate sparse codes.
Investigating JumpReLU variants that apply a threshold on both positive and negative activations.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as powerful techniques for interpretability of large language models (LLMs), aiming to decompose hidden states into meaningful semantic features. While several SAE variants have been proposed, there remains no principled framework to derive SAEs from the original dictionary learning formulation. In this work, we introduce such a framework by unrolling the proximal gradient method for sparse coding. We show that a single-step update naturally recovers common SAE variants, including ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. Through this lens, we reveal a fundamental limitation of existing SAEs: their sparsity-inducing regularizers enforce non-negativity, preventing a single feature from representing bidirectional concepts (e.g., male vs. female). This structural constraint fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness. To address this issue, we propose AbsTopK SAE, a new variant derived from the $\ell_0$ sparsity constraint that applies hard thresholding over the largest-magnitude activations. By preserving both positive and negative activations, AbsTopK uncovers richer, bidirectional conceptual representations. Comprehensive experiments across four LLMs and seven probing and steering tasks show that AbsTopK improves reconstruction fidelity, enhances interpretability, and enables single features to encode contrasting concepts. Remarkably, AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the Difference-in-Mean method, a supervised approach that requires labeled data for each concept and has been shown in prior work to outperform SAEs.

papers.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be improved to reduce biases like shrinkage and achieve better sparsity and reconstruction fidelity in language model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gated SAEs that decouple feature detection and magnitude estimation, solving shrinkage and providing Pareto improvements in sparsity and reconstruction fidelity over baseline SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Gated SAEs are a promising improvement for sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability, offering better performance and reduced biases.
papers.key_findings:
Gated SAEs achieve better reconstruction fidelity at any given level of sparsity compared to baseline SAEs.
Gated SAEs effectively address the shrinkage problem, with reconstructions being unbiased.
Gated SAE features are similarly interpretable to baseline SAE features based on human evaluation.
Ablation studies show that freezing the decoder in the auxiliary task and weight tying are important for performance.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are an effective technique for unsupervised discovery of interpretable features in language models' (LMs) activations, by finding sparse, linear reconstructions of LM activations. We introduce the Gated Sparse Autoencoder (Gated SAE), which achieves a Pareto improvement over training with prevailing methods. In SAEs, the L1 penalty used to encourage sparsity introduces many undesirable biases, such as shrinkage -- systematic underestimation of feature activations. The key insight of Gated SAEs is to separate the functionality of (a) determining which directions to use and (b) estimating the magnitudes of those directions: this enables us to apply the L1 penalty only to the former, limiting the scope of undesirable side effects. Through training SAEs on LMs of up to 7B parameters we find that, in typical hyper-parameter ranges, Gated SAEs solve shrinkage, are similarly interpretable, and require half as many firing features to achieve comparable reconstruction fidelity.

papers.title: Beyond Activation Patterns: A Weight-Based Out-of-Context Explanation of Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we interpret Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features from a weight-based, out-of-context perspective to understand their computational roles, beyond activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a weight-based, out-of-context interpretation framework for SAE features that reveals their computational roles in output prediction and attention mechanisms, complementing activation-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Weight-based, out-of-context analysis provides the missing half of SAE feature interpretability, revealing computational roles and depth-dependent functional specialization that activation patterns alone cannot capture.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 1/4 of SAE features directly predict output tokens when analyzed through their decoder-unembedding interactions.
Semantic features exhibit a U-shaped distribution across depth in Gemma models (high in early and late layers) and a monotonic distribution in Llama models, revealing architectural differences in functional specialization.
Features actively participate in attention mechanisms, with pre- and post-softmax analysis showing depth-dependent structure and distinct profiles for semantic vs. non-semantic populations.
Weight-based analysis uncovers that early-layer features in Llama specialize for input token recognition (encoder-embedding alignment) while late-layer features specialize for output prediction (decoder-unembedding alignment).
The out-of-context framework provides a complementary, causal perspective on feature function that activation-based methods miss.
papers.limitation:
The out-of-context framework is strict and simulates attention competition across the entire SAE dictionary, which may not reflect the contextual sparsity of actual forward passes and could underestimate feature importance.
The analysis focuses on intra-layer attention (features in layer L interacting with QK circuits in layer L+1) and may miss features specialized for longer-range, inter-layer interactions.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful technique for decomposing language model representations into interpretable features. Current interpretation methods infer feature semantics from activation patterns, but overlook that features are trained to reconstruct activations that serve computational roles in the forward pass. We introduce a novel weight-based interpretation framework that measures functional effects through direct weight interactions, requiring no activation data. Through three experiments on Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 models, we demonstrate that (1) 1/4 of features directly predict output tokens, (2) features actively participate in attention mechanisms with depth-dependent structure, and (3) semantic and non-semantic feature populations exhibit distinct distribution profiles in attention circuits. Our analysis provides the missing out-of-context half of SAE feature interpretability.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: PolySAE: Modeling Feature Interactions in Sparse Autoencoders via Polynomial Decoding
papers.research_question: How can we extend sparse autoencoders to model non-linear feature interactions (compositional structure) while preserving a linear encoder for interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PolySAE, a sparse autoencoder that extends the decoder with quadratic and cubic terms to model feature interactions via low-rank tensor factorization, improving feature separation and probing performance while maintaining reconstruction fidelity.
papers.conclusion: PolySAE effectively models feature interactions in sparse autoencoders, capturing compositional structure beyond linear combinations and improving interpretability without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
papers.key_findings:
PolySAE achieves an average improvement of approximately 8% in probing F1 across four language models and three SAE variants while maintaining comparable reconstruction error.
PolySAE produces 2–10× larger Wasserstein distances between class-conditional feature distributions, indicating more separated semantic structure.
Learned interaction weights exhibit negligible correlation with co-occurrence frequency (r=0.06), suggesting they capture compositional structure rather than surface statistics.
PolySAE adds a small parameter overhead (3% for GPT-2 small) through low-rank factorization of interaction terms.
Qualitative analysis shows PolySAE captures compositional structures like morphological binding (e.g., 'administrators') and phrasal composition (e.g., 'Starbucks').
papers.limitation: The study is limited to models up to 2B parameters and experiments are restricted to forced-sparsity SAE variants.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method for interpreting neural network representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of dictionary atoms. However, SAEs assume that features combine additively through linear reconstruction, an assumption that cannot capture compositional structure: linear models cannot distinguish whether "Starbucks" arises from the composition of "star" and "coffee" features or merely their co-occurrence. This forces SAEs to allocate monolithic features for compound concepts rather than decomposing them into interpretable constituents. We introduce PolySAE, which extends the SAE decoder with higher-order terms to model feature interactions while preserving the linear encoder essential for interpretability. Through low-rank tensor factorization on a shared projection subspace, PolySAE captures pairwise and triple feature interactions with small parameter overhead (3% on GPT2). Across four language models and three SAE variants, PolySAE achieves an average improvement of approximately 8% in probing F1 while maintaining comparable reconstruction error, and produces 2-10$\times$ larger Wasserstein distances between class-conditional feature distributions. Critically, learned interaction weights exhibit negligible correlation with co-occurrence frequency ($r = 0.06$ vs. $r = 0.82$ for SAE feature covariance), suggesting that polynomial terms capture compositional structure, such as morphological binding and phrasal composition, largely independent of surface statistics.

papers.title: Evaluating Adversarial Robustness of Concept Representations in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of concept representations in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to adversarial input perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces robustness as a critical evaluation dimension for sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and demonstrates that SAE concept representations are vulnerable to adversarial input perturbations.
papers.conclusion: SAE interpretations are highly vulnerable to minimal input changes, raising concerns about their reliability in realistic settings, and motivating the development of more robust interpretability tools.
papers.key_findings:
Small adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate SAE concept representations without notably affecting the base LLM's activations.
SAE concept representations are not robust even to non-adversarial synonym replacements.
The attacks are effective across different models, datasets, and model depths.
Untargeted attacks are more successful at the population level, while targeted attacks are more effective at the individual level.
SAE latents that represent meaningful concepts are highly manipulable.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of attacks is bounded by compute constraints (single 80GB A100 GPU).
The choice of medium-sized LLMs results in slower attacks.
future_direction: Developing novel methods to denoise SAE activations and isolate reliable signals.
Extending the evaluation framework to other concept-extraction tools like transcoders and crosscoders.
Optimizing the attack pipeline to better balance effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are commonly used to interpret the internal activations of large language models (LLMs) by mapping them to human-interpretable concept representations. While existing evaluations of SAEs focus on metrics such as the reconstruction-sparsity tradeoff, human (auto-)interpretability, and feature disentanglement, they overlook a critical aspect: the robustness of concept representations to input perturbations. We argue that robustness must be a fundamental consideration for concept representations, reflecting the fidelity of concept labeling. To this end, we formulate robustness quantification as input-space optimization problems and develop a comprehensive evaluation framework featuring realistic scenarios in which adversarial perturbations are crafted to manipulate SAE representations. Empirically, we find that tiny adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate concept-based interpretations in most scenarios without notably affecting the base LLM's activations. Overall, our results suggest that SAE concept representations are fragile and without further denoising or postprocessing they might be ill-suited for applications in model monitoring and oversight.

papers.title: On the Theoretical Understanding of Identifiable Sparse Autoencoders and Beyond
papers.research_question: Can SAEs recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the polysemantic inputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical framework showing that standard Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) generally fail to fully recover ground-truth monosemantic features unless they are extremely sparse, and proposes a reweighted SAE (WSAE) that improves feature recovery by adaptively weighting dimensions based on their polysemantic level.
papers.conclusion: SAEs have inherent limits and cannot fully disentangle features under realistic sparsity; they should be regarded as an approximation tool. The proposed WSAE enhances feature recovery and interpretability in low-sparsity scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs generally fail to fully recover ground truth monosemantic features due to feature shrinking and feature vanishing.
SAEs can fully recover ground truth features only under the condition of extreme sparsity.
The proposed Weighted Sparse Autoencoder (WSAE) narrows the gap between polysemantic feature reconstruction and ground truth feature reconstruction, leading to better recovery.
Experiments on synthetic data validate the theoretical findings on sparsity and the improvement from reweighting.
Experiments on real language (Pythia, Llama) and vision (ResNet) models show that WSAE enhances feature monosemanticity and interpretability compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation: SAE-based interpretability should be regarded as an approximation tool, not as a faithful feature recovery mechanism, because full disentanglement is mathematically impossible under realistic sparsity.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting features learned by large language models (LLMs). It aims to recover complex superposed polysemantic features into interpretable monosemantic ones through feature reconstruction via sparsely activated neural networks. Despite the wide applications of SAEs, it remains unclear under what conditions an SAE can fully recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the superposed polysemantic ones. In this paper, through theoretical analysis, we for the first time propose the necessary and sufficient conditions for identifiable SAEs (SAEs that learn unique and ground truth monosemantic features), including 1) extreme sparsity of the ground truth feature, 2) sparse activation of SAEs, and 3) enough hidden dimensions of SAEs. Moreover, when the identifiable conditions are not fully met, we propose a reweighting strategy to improve the identifiability. Specifically, following the theoretically suggested weight selection principle, we prove that the gap between the loss functions of SAE reconstruction and monosemantic feature reconstruction can be narrowed, so that the reweighted SAEs have better reconstruction of the ground truth monosemantic features than the uniformly weighted ones. In experiments, we validate our theoretical findings and show that our weighted SAE significantly improves feature monosemanticity and interpretability.

papers.title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the extent of feature space universality across large language models? Specifically, whether SAE feature spaces are similar under rotation-invariant transformations.
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that SAE feature spaces are similar across different LLMs, supporting the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which enables the transfer of interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that feature spaces are universal across LLMs, providing evidence for the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which can facilitate the transfer of interpretability techniques like steering vectors.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of LLMs show the highest similarity in SAE feature spaces, while layer 0 has low similarity.
Semantically meaningful subspaces, such as those for emotions or time, exhibit notable similarity across models.
The similarity is statistically significant as measured by SVCCA and RSA, with p-values below 0.05 for most layer pairs.
The approach works across various model pairs, including Pythia, Gemma, and Llama models.
Filtering non-concept features and many-to-1 mappings improves similarity scores.
papers.abstract: The Universality Hypothesis in large language models (LLMs) claims that different models converge towards similar concept representations in their latent spaces. Providing evidence for this hypothesis would enable researchers to exploit universal properties, facilitating the generalization of mechanistic interpretability techniques across models. Previous works studied if LLMs learned the same features, which are internal representations that activate on specific concepts. Since comparing features across LLMs is challenging due to polysemanticity, in which LLM neurons often correspond to multiple unrelated features rather than to distinct concepts, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been employed to disentangle LLM neurons into SAE features corresponding to distinct concepts. In this paper, we introduce a new variation of the universality hypothesis called Analogous Feature Universality: we hypothesize that even if SAEs across different models learn different feature representations, the spaces spanned by SAE features are similar, such that one SAE space is similar to another SAE space under rotation-invariant transformations. Evidence for this hypothesis would imply that interpretability techniques related to latent spaces, such as steering vectors, may be transferred across models via certain transformations. To investigate this hypothesis, we first pair SAE features across different models via activation correlation, and then measure spatial relation similarities between paired features via representational similarity measures, which transform spaces into representations that reveal hidden relational similarities. Our experiments demonstrate high similarities for SAE feature spaces across various LLMs, providing evidence for feature space universality.

papers.title: Deep Learning of Part-Based Representation of Data Using Sparse Autoencoders With Nonnegativity Constraints
papers.research_question: How can nonnegativity constraints in autoencoder training be used to learn part-based representations of data, and does this improve reconstruction and prediction performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a nonnegativity constraint algorithm (NCAE) for training autoencoders that learns part-based, sparse features, improving reconstruction quality and the prediction performance of deep networks.
papers.conclusion: Nonnegativity constraints in autoencoder training enable part-based representation learning, which improves reconstruction and classification performance in deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Nonnegativity constraints force autoencoders to learn features that capture a part-based representation of data.
NCAE achieves lower reconstruction error and better sparsity in hidden encoding compared to SAE and NMF.
A deep network pre-trained with NCAE achieves better classification accuracy than networks pre-trained with SAE, NNSAE, DAE, and DpAE on several datasets.
The learned features (receptive fields) are more interpretable, representing parts like strokes in digits or facial features.
The method works for both image and text data, extracting semantic features from documents.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a new deep learning autoencoder network, trained by a nonnegativity constraint algorithm (nonnegativity-constrained autoencoder), that learns features that show part-based representation of data. The learning algorithm is based on constraining negative weights. The performance of the algorithm is assessed based on decomposing data into parts and its prediction performance is tested on three standard image data sets and one text data set. The results indicate that the nonnegativity constraint forces the autoencoder to learn features that amount to a part-based representation of data, while improving sparsity and reconstruction quality in comparison with the traditional sparse autoencoder and nonnegative matrix factorization. It is also shown that this newly acquired representation improves the prediction performance of a deep neural network.

papers.title: Llama Scope: Extracting Millions of Features from Llama-3.1-8B with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scalably train Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on large language models, and how do these SAEs perform in terms of sparsity-fidelity trade-off, interpretability, and generalization to longer contexts and fine-tuned models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Llama Scope, a suite of 256 Sparse Autoencoders trained on every layer and sublayer of Llama-3.1-8B-Base, along with modifications to Top-K SAEs and a scalable training infrastructure, providing a resource for mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Llama Scope provides a comprehensive set of SAEs that advance the Pareto frontier of sparsity and reconstruction fidelity, and the SAEs generalize effectively to out-of-distribution settings, facilitating future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
TopK SAEs outperform vanilla SAEs in sparsity-fidelity trade-off.
Wider SAEs (with more features) achieve better reconstruction quality at the same sparsity level.
SAEs trained on base models generalize well to longer contexts and instruction-finetuned models.
Feature geometry analysis confirms that feature splitting enables the discovery of new features.
The firing frequency distribution of SAE features is consistent with expected sparsity constraints.
papers.limitation:
The monosemanticity evaluation focuses on top activations and may not capture behavior on low-activating samples.
The online activation generation method can lead to redundant computation when training multiple SAEs on the same position.
future_direction: Exploring SAE-based circuit analysis and fine-grained causal analysis.
Conducting automated prompt-based evaluations across a wide range of tasks.
Fine-tuning SAEs for long-context data.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful unsupervised method for extracting sparse representations from language models, yet scalable training remains a significant challenge. We introduce a suite of 256 SAEs, trained on each layer and sublayer of the Llama-3.1-8B-Base model, with 32K and 128K features. Modifications to a state-of-the-art SAE variant, Top-K SAEs, are evaluated across multiple dimensions. In particular, we assess the generalizability of SAEs trained on base models to longer contexts and fine-tuned models. Additionally, we analyze the geometry of learned SAE latents, confirming that \emph{feature splitting} enables the discovery of new features. The Llama Scope SAE checkpoints are publicly available at~\url{https://huggingface.co/fnlp/Llama-Scope}, alongside our scalable training, interpretation, and visualization tools at \url{https://github.com/OpenMOSS/Language-Model-SAEs}. These contributions aim to advance the open-source Sparse Autoencoder ecosystem and support mechanistic interpretability research by reducing the need for redundant SAE training.

papers.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we train sparse autoencoders to learn hierarchical features and avoid pathologies like feature absorption and splitting when scaling dictionary size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders, a hierarchical variant that trains multiple nested dictionaries simultaneously to learn features at different levels of abstraction, reducing feature absorption and splitting.
