ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Sparse Semantic Dimension as a Generalization Certificate for LLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) generalize robustly despite having parameter counts that vastly exceed the number of training tokens? The paper investigates whether the effective capacity controlling generalization lies in the low-dimensional, sparse geometry of the model's internal representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that the effective complexity of LLMs is governed by the sparse, low-dimensional manifold of internal representations, and introduces the Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD) to provide non-vacuous generalization bounds that scale with the active feature pool rather than the parameter count.
papers.conclusion: The Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD) resolves the generalization paradox by shifting the complexity measure from parameter count to the active feature pool, providing a mathematical certificate for generalization and a safety monitor for OOD detection via feature density.
papers.key_findings:
The SSD-based generalization bound becomes non-vacuous at realistic sample sizes (e.g., N≈50,000) for GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B, where parameter-counting bounds would be vacuous.
Larger models (Gemma-2B) require significantly fewer calibration samples to identify their active manifold than smaller models (GPT-2), suggesting they learn more compressible, distinct semantic structures.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs trigger a measurable 'feature explosion' (a sharp spike in active features), which serves as a reliable, computationally cheap proxy for epistemic uncertainty and can function as a safety monitor.
The generalization guarantee depends on the specific semantic alignment of activated SAE features, not just statistical sparsity, as shown by an ablation where shuffling feature indices causes a catastrophic increase in reconstruction error.
The framework decomposes generalization into interpretable components: empirical risk, reconstruction error, pool mismatch, and a complexity penalty based on the active concept pool size.
future_direction: Investigate how the ratio of SSD to parameter count evolves for frontier-scale models (e.g., 70B+ parameters) and whether a 'sparsity saturation' point exists.
Investigate layer-wise generalization dynamics by using SAEs at different layers to determine which layers govern memorization versus generalization.
Extend the theoretical bounds to account for dynamic or context-dependent concept pools to provide tighter guarantees for models operating in rapidly shifting domains.
papers.abstract: Standard statistical learning theory predicts that Large Language Models (LLMs) should overfit because their parameter counts vastly exceed the number of training tokens. Yet, in practice, they generalize robustly. We propose that the effective capacity controlling generalization lies in the geometry of the model's internal representations: while the parameter space is high-dimensional, the activation states lie on a low-dimensional, sparse manifold. To formalize this, we introduce the Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD), a complexity measure derived from the active feature vocabulary of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on the model's layers. Treating the LLM and SAE as frozen oracles, we utilize this framework to attribute the model's generalization capabilities to the sparsity of the dictionary rather than the total parameter count. Empirically, we validate this framework on GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B, demonstrating that our bound provides non-vacuous certificates at realistic sample sizes. Crucially, we uncover a counter-intuitive "feature sharpness" scaling law: despite being an order of magnitude larger, Gemma-2B requires significantly fewer calibration samples to identify its active manifold compared to GPT-2, suggesting that larger models learn more compressible, distinct semantic structures. Finally, we show that this framework functions as a reliable safety monitor: out-of-distribution inputs trigger a measurable "feature explosion" (a sharp spike in active features), effectively signaling epistemic uncertainty through learned feature violation. Code is available at: https://github.com/newcodevelop/sparse-semantic-dimension.

papers.title: Adaptive Sparse Allocation with Mutual Choice & Feature Choice Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be improved to allow adaptive computation and reduce dead features by variable allocation of sparsity budget per token and per feature?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Feature Choice and Mutual Choice SAEs, which allow adaptive computation by variable allocation of sparsity budget, and aux_zipf_loss, reducing dead features and improving reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: Feature Choice and Mutual Choice SAEs are simple drop-in improvements that enable adaptive computation and reduce dead features, advancing sparse autoencoder training for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Feature Choice and Mutual Choice SAEs achieve better reconstruction loss at equivalent sparsity levels compared to TopK SAEs.
Feature Choice SAEs result in zero dead features even at large scale, without complex resampling.
The aux_zipf_loss mitigates underutilized features and helps utilize SAE capacity more fully.
Feature densities in SAEs tend to follow a Zipf distribution, and constraining with Zipf distribution outperforms uniform distribution.
Adaptive computation allows difficult tokens to use more features and easy tokens to use fewer.
papers.limitation:
Appeals to the Monotonic Importance Heuristic may miss important low-magnitude activations.
Generalisation across modalities (e.g., audio, images) is untested.
Lack of widely agreed upon metrics for evaluating sparse autoencoders.
future_direction: Scaling laws for Feature Choice SAE performance on larger models.
Dissecting phenomenology of features conditioning on prevalence and activation magnitude.
Applying similar techniques to interpretability problems in other modalities.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach to extracting features from neural networks, enabling model interpretability as well as causal interventions on model internals. SAEs generate sparse feature representations using a sparsifying activation function that implicitly defines a set of token-feature matches. We frame the token-feature matching as a resource allocation problem constrained by a total sparsity upper bound. For example, TopK SAEs solve this allocation problem with the additional constraint that each token matches with at most $k$ features. In TopK SAEs, the $k$ active features per token constraint is the same across tokens, despite some tokens being more difficult to reconstruct than others. To address this limitation, we propose two novel SAE variants, Feature Choice SAEs and Mutual Choice SAEs, which each allow for a variable number of active features per token. Feature Choice SAEs solve the sparsity allocation problem under the additional constraint that each feature matches with at most $m$ tokens. Mutual Choice SAEs solve the unrestricted allocation problem where the total sparsity budget can be allocated freely between tokens and features. Additionally, we introduce a new auxiliary loss function, $\mathtt{aux\_zipf\_loss}$, which generalises the $\mathtt{aux\_k\_loss}$ to mitigate dead and underutilised features. Our methods result in SAEs with fewer dead features and improved reconstruction loss at equivalent sparsity levels as a result of the inherent adaptive computation. More accurate and scalable feature extraction methods provide a path towards better understanding and more precise control of foundation models.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of Sparse Autoencoder and Activation Difference in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve language model steering by selecting the most relevant sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and applying a token-wise decaying steering strategy to avoid degenerate outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method to select the most relevant SAE feature for steering and introduces a token-wise decaying steering strategy, which improves stability and performance in mathematical reasoning and instruction following tasks.
papers.conclusion: Decaying SAE steering is an effective method for controlling language model behavior, providing a more interpretable alternative to mean activation difference, especially in mathematical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE steering with a single relevant feature and decaying strategy outperforms constant steering and mean activation difference in math reasoning.
SAE steering can elicit step-by-step mathematical reasoning without few-shot prompts.
In instruction following, SAE steering matches the performance of mean activation difference.
The proposed feature selection method effectively removes redundant SAE features.
Decaying steering avoids degenerate outputs such as repetitive words.
papers.limitation:
The proposed method struggles with word inclusion tasks, as no single SAE feature reliably encodes lexical constraints.
The explanations from Neuronpedia are not guaranteed to be precise.
future_direction: Finer-grained SAE combinations for language proximity cases.
Multilingual-aware alignment strategies for steering.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for language model steering. Prior work has explored top-k SAE latents for steering, but we observe that many dimensions among the top-k latents capture non-semantic features such as punctuation rather than semantic attributes like instructions. To address this, we propose focusing on a single, most relevant SAE latent (top-1), eliminating redundant features. We further identify a limitation in constant SAE steering, which often produces degenerate outputs such as repetitive single words. To mitigate this, we introduce a token-wise decaying steering strategy, enabling more faithful comparisons with mean activation difference baselines. Empirically, we show that steering an SAE latent associated with reasoning reliably elicits step-by-step mathematical reasoning and enhances inference quality, functionally resembling the effect of appending a guiding token. Our results demonstrate that SAEs outperform mean activation difference methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and match their performance on IF-Eval.

papers.title: Measuring Feature Sparsity in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we measure the success of sparse coding techniques in language models, and to what extent do language model activations adhere to the linearity and sparsity assumptions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces metrics to measure feature sparsity in language models and provides evidence that activations are sparse linear combinations of features, with sparsity highest in the first and final layers.
papers.conclusion: Activations across various model architectures and all layers were more sparse than several control datasets, providing evidence for the linearity and sparsity hypotheses, and activation sparsity is greatest in the first and final layers of a model.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed metrics (average coefficient norm and normalized loss) can reliably distinguish sparse linear data from other distributions and predict sparsity levels in synthetic data.
Language model embeddings are more sparse than Gaussian distributions, supporting the linearity and sparsity hypotheses.
Sparsity levels vary with embedding size and architecture (BERT vs TinyStories).
Across layers in BERT models, sparsity is highest in the embedding layer, decreases in middle layers, and increases again in final layers.
The feature directions found by sparse coding correspond to interpretable features (e.g., for tokens like 'season' and 'physics').
future_direction: More rigorous tests of the linearity and sparsity hypotheses
Further investigations into factors affecting superposition
Improved methods to disentangle superposed features
papers.abstract: Recent works have proposed that activations in language models can be modelled as sparse linear combinations of vectors corresponding to features of input text. Under this assumption, these works aimed to reconstruct feature directions using sparse coding. We develop metrics to assess the success of these sparse coding techniques and test the validity of the linearity and sparsity assumptions. We show our metrics can predict the level of sparsity on synthetic sparse linear activations, and can distinguish between sparse linear data and several other distributions. We use our metrics to measure levels of sparsity in several language models. We find evidence that language model activations can be accurately modelled by sparse linear combinations of features, significantly more so than control datasets. We also show that model activations appear to be sparsest in the first and final layers.

papers.title: FaithfulSAE: Towards Capturing Faithful Features with Sparse Autoencoders without External Dataset Dependencies
papers.research_question: How does training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on out-of-distribution data affect their stability and feature faithfulness, and can training on the model's own synthetic data improve these aspects?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FaithfulSAE, a method to train Sparse Autoencoders on the model's own synthetic data, which improves feature stability and reduces fake features compared to training on external datasets.
papers.conclusion: Training SAEs on the model's own synthetic data (FaithfulSAE) improves feature consistency and reduces fake features, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features.
papers.key_findings:
FaithfulSAEs trained on synthetic data show higher stability across seeds compared to SAEs trained on instruction datasets.
FaithfulSAEs achieve lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models compared to web-based dataset trained SAEs.
FaithfulSAEs outperform web-based SAEs in SAE probing tasks, indicating better reconstruction of the model's hidden state.
Shared Feature Ratio is higher when the target model and source model for synthetic data are the same, indicating that SAE training on its own data is more stable.
papers.limitation:
Lack of evaluation on instruction-tuned or reasoning models.
Shared Feature Ratio may not fully reflect the complexity of high-dimensional feature spaces.
Did not assess the interpretability of individual features through case studies.
future_direction: Exploring improved dataset generation and training strategies that could completely outperform Web-based methods.
Evaluating whether Faithful SAEs provide meaningful and interpretable explanations for individual features through detailed case studies.
Investigating the connection between pruning Fake Features and the principle of Minimal Description Length.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising solution for decomposing large language model representations into interpretable features. However, Paulo and Belrose (2025) have highlighted instability across different initialization seeds, and Heap et al. (2025) have pointed out that SAEs may not capture model-internal features. These problems likely stem from training SAEs on external datasets - either collected from the Web or generated by another model - which may contain out-of-distribution (OOD) data beyond the model's generalisation capabilities. This can result in hallucinated SAE features, which we term "Fake Features", that misrepresent the model's internal activations. To address these issues, we propose FaithfulSAE, a method that trains SAEs on the model's own synthetic dataset. Using FaithfulSAEs, we demonstrate that training SAEs on less-OOD instruction datasets results in SAEs being more stable across seeds. Notably, FaithfulSAEs outperform SAEs trained on web-based datasets in the SAE probing task and exhibit a lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models. Overall, our approach eliminates the dependency on external datasets, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features while highlighting the often neglected importance of SAE training datasets.

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FF-KV features achieve comparable interpretability to SAE features across multiple automatic evaluation metrics from SAEBENCH.
FF-KV features sometimes outperform SAEs, e.g., in absorption (less redundancy) and explained variance (perfect by definition).
Human evaluation shows conceptual features can be found with almost equal ease from both FF-KV and SAEs.
Features discovered by proxy methods (e.g., Transcoders) often do not align with features in the original FF module, suggesting potential hallucination.
Increasing sparsity in FF-KV (via TopK) does not consistently improve interpretability across metrics.
papers.limitation:
SCR and TPP scores are highly unstable and should be treated as supplementary results.
The theoretical advantage of SAEs is not observed empirically through the current evaluation scheme.
future_direction: Further research on the faithfulness of learned features from proxy modules, with FF-KV features as grounding points.
Inclusion of FF-KV features as a baseline when assessing feature-discovery methods in interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

papers.title: Unveiling Decision-Making in LLMs for Text Classification : Extraction of influential and interpretable concepts with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) based explainability approaches for sentence classification, and can a novel supervised SAE variant (ClassifSAE) improve the causality and interpretability of extracted concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ClassifSAE, a supervised Sparse Autoencoder variant for text classification that extracts more interpretable and causal concepts from LLMs, and proposes two new metrics (ConceptSim and SentenceSim) for evaluating concept precision.
papers.conclusion: ClassifSAE is an effective method for extracting interpretable and causal concepts from LLMs for text classification, offering a good trade-off between interpretability and causality.
papers.key_findings:
ClassifSAE produces concepts with higher interpretability (ConceptSim) and better sparsity than baselines.
ClassifSAE achieves second-best causality scores (after HI-Concept) but with better interpretability.
ClassifSAE is computationally more efficient, requiring up to 83% less training time than HI-Concept.
The joint classifier and activation rate sparsity loss in ClassifSAE improve disentanglement and sparsity of concepts.
ClassifSAE can identify fine-grained concepts beyond coarse label categories.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been successfully used to probe Large Language Models (LLMs) and extract interpretable concepts from their internal representations. These concepts are linear combinations of neuron activations that correspond to human-interpretable features. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of SAE-based explainability approaches for sentence classification, a domain where such methods have not been extensively explored. We present a novel SAE-based model ClassifSAE tailored for text classification, leveraging a specialized classifier head and incorporating an activation rate sparsity loss. We benchmark this architecture against established methods such as ConceptShap, Independent Component Analysis, HI-Concept and a standard TopK-SAE baseline. Our evaluation covers several classification benchmarks and backbone LLMs. We further enrich our analysis with two novel metrics for measuring the precision of concept-based explanations, using an external sentence encoder. Our empirical results show that ClassifSAE improves both the causality and interpretability of the extracted features.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators: Model Recovery in Function Spaces
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be extended to operate in infinite-dimensional function spaces for concept learning, and what advantages do functional representations offer over standard SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse autoencoder neural operators (SAE-NOs) that operate in function spaces, specifically SAE-FNOs, which improve concept learning stability, robustness, and generalization compared to standard SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Functional representations in SAE-NOs extend sparse autoencoders from detectors of concept presence to models that capture the underlying structure of the data, highlighting parameterization as a central driver of interpretability and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-FNO successfully recovers ground-truth concepts in synthetic data and converges to zero dictionary recovery error.
SAE-FNO generalizes to unseen input resolutions, unlike SAE-CNN which fails beyond training resolution.
SAE-FNO learns concepts that are stable across different sparsity levels and exhibit diverse correlations, overcoming the orthogonality bias of SAE-MLP.
SAE-FNO achieves higher concept utilization efficiency, requiring fewer concepts to represent data, especially for larger domains.
Lifting accelerates concept recovery by acting as a preconditioner and improves optimization.
papers.abstract: We frame the problem of unifying representations in neural models as one of sparse model recovery and introduce a framework that extends sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to lifted spaces and infinite-dimensional function spaces, enabling mechanistic interpretability of large neural operators (NO). While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that neural networks converge to similar representations across architectures, the representational properties of neural operators remain underexplored despite their growing importance in scientific computing. We compare the inference and training dynamics of SAEs, lifted-SAE, and SAE neural operators. We highlight how lifting and operator modules introduce beneficial inductive biases, enabling faster recovery, improved recovery of smooth concepts, and robust inference across varying resolutions, a property unique to neural operators.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret the internal representations of protein language models and steer them to generate sequences with desired features?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can be applied to protein language models to interpret their internal representations and that the identified latent features can be used to steer the model to generate protein sequences with desired structural motifs.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders provide a promising approach for interpreting and controlling protein language models, opening new avenues for protein design and engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders trained on ESM-2 activations can identify latent components associated with protein annotations such as transmembrane regions, binding sites, and zinc finger motifs.
A heuristic based on intrinsic dimension estimation can guide the selection of the transformer layer from which to extract representations for SAE training.
Intervening on specific latent components during inference can steer the model to generate protein sequences that contain desired features, such as zinc finger domains.
The sequence generation pipeline successfully produced sequences with zinc finger motifs, though it requires parameter tuning to improve success rates.
papers.limitation:
The sequence generation pipeline requires parameter fine-tuning to improve the success rate.
The features learned by the model may not directly align with manually curated dataset annotations, as latents might encode more specific or coarse-grained features.
future_direction: Extend these methods to larger models and a wider range of protein features.
Automate the parameter search for the sequence generation pipeline to improve efficiency.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancements in transformer-based language models have revolutionized natural language processing, yet understanding the internal mechanisms of these models remains a significant challenge. This paper explores the application of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to interpret the internal representations of protein language models, specifically focusing on the ESM-2 8M parameter model. By performing a statistical analysis on each latent component's relevance to distinct protein annotations, we identify potential interpretations linked to various protein characteristics, including transmembrane regions, binding sites, and specialized motifs. We then leverage these insights to guide sequence generation, shortlisting the relevant latent components that can steer the model towards desired targets such as zinc finger domains. This work contributes to the emerging field of mechanistic interpretability in biological sequence models, offering new perspectives on model steering for sequence design.

papers.title: Binary Sparse Coding for Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does binarising sparse autoencoder activations improve the interpretability and monosemanticity of the discovered features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces binary sparse autoencoders and transcoders, finding that binarisation improves unweighted feature interpretability but increases reconstruction error and ultra-high frequency features, suggesting polysemanticity may be an ineliminable property of neural activations.
papers.conclusion: Binary sparse coders are not recommended for most purposes; the attempt to eliminate polysemanticity by binarising activations merely shifted it to high-frequency features, supporting the idea that polysemanticity is ineliminable.
papers.key_findings:
Binarisation improves unweighted average feature interpretability but increases the cross-entropy loss when patched into the base model.
Binarisation does not increase interpretability when features are weighted by their firing frequencies.
Binary transcoders have more ultra-high frequency features than continuous ones, and these tend to have low interpretability scores.
Binary sparse coders underperform continuous ones in sparse probing evaluation before fine-tuning, but after fine-tuning they outperform.
There is little relationship between interpretability and causal importance of features except at the extremes of interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single dataset (SmolLM2 training corpus) may limit applicability.
Some sparse coders exhibited high numbers of dead neurons.
Results may change at higher sparse coder widths.
future_direction: Exploring mixed architectures with a mixture of binary and continuous features.
Dynamically determining the appropriate mixture of binary and continuous features in a data-dependent way.
Further investigation of the promising performance of binary sparse coders on sparse probing tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to decompose neural network activations into sparsely activating features, but many SAE features are only interpretable at high activation strengths. To address this issue we propose to use binary sparse autoencoders (BAEs) and binary transcoders (BTCs), which constrain all activations to be zero or one. We find that binarisation significantly improves the interpretability and monosemanticity of the discovered features, while increasing reconstruction error. By eliminating the distinction between high and low activation strengths, we prevent uninterpretable information from being smuggled in through the continuous variation in feature activations. However, we also find that binarisation increases the number of uninterpretable ultra-high frequency features, and when interpretability scores are frequency-adjusted, the scores for continuous sparse coders are slightly better than those of binary ones. This suggests that polysemanticity may be an ineliminable property of neural activations.

papers.title: Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding through Numerical Attributes in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally integrate multiple numerical attributes of a single entity? How does irrelevant numerical context perturb these representations and their downstream outputs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode numerical attributes in shared linear subspaces, amplify real-world correlations, and are vulnerable to irrelevant numerical context, with smaller models being more susceptible.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal vulnerabilities in LLM decision-making under multi-attribute entanglement and lay groundwork for fairer, representation-aware control in numerically-sensitive applications.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode multiple numerical attributes of an entity in overlapping internal subspaces.
Internal correlations between attributes can exceed the natural correlations observed in the data.
Asymmetric interference patterns exist where certain dominant attributes exert disproportionate influence over others in the representation.
Irrelevant numerical context in prompts perturbs internal representations and degrades output reliability, especially in smaller models.
Larger models are more robust to such perturbations, likely due to more complex computations.
papers.limitation:
The method does not scale to multiple concurrent confounders and is limited by a single-confounder assumption.
The study focused only on fact-retrieval tasks and did not explore arithmetic reasoning under in-context learning.
No single subspace was identified that uniformly represents arbitrary numerical features.
future_direction: Employ multivariate causal inference or factor-analytic techniques to disentangle complex attribute relationships.
Conduct a broader study including generative and multi-step arithmetic reasoning scenarios.
papers.abstract: Although behavioral studies have documented numerical reasoning errors in large language models (LLMs), the underlying representational mechanisms remain unclear. We hypothesize that numerical attributes occupy shared latent subspaces and investigate two questions:(1) How do LLMs internally integrate multiple numerical attributes of a single entity? (2)How does irrelevant numerical context perturb these representations and their downstream outputs? To address these questions, we combine linear probing with partial correlation analysis and prompt-based vulnerability tests across models of varying sizes. Our results show that LLMs encode real-world numerical correlations but tend to systematically amplify them. Moreover, irrelevant context induces consistent shifts in magnitude representations, with downstream effects that vary by model size. These findings reveal a vulnerability in LLM decision-making and lay the groundwork for fairer, representation-aware control under multi-attribute entanglement.

papers.title: How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual: Tracing Internal Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do bilingual language models develop internal representations, specifically when, where, and how does bilingual alignment emerge during pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: Bilingual language models first learn languages separately and then gradually form bilingual alignments, particularly in mid-layers, with larger models showing stronger alignment; bilingual representations are critical for performance, as shown by an intervention method that injects bilingual features from a fully trained model into a mid-training model.
papers.conclusion: Bilingual language models initially learn languages independently and later develop bilingual alignments, especially in mid-layers of larger models, and sparse autoencoders can be used for both analysis and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs initially learn languages independently and gradually develop bilingual alignment over training.
Bilingual alignments are more prominently captured in the mid-layers of the model.
Larger models exhibit stronger bilingual alignment than smaller ones.
Bilingual representations from a fully trained model enhance the performance of a mid-training model when injected.
The model's internal representations evolve from language-specific to bilingual semantic alignment as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on English and Japanese, so findings may not generalize to all language pairs.
The interpretability of sparse autoencoders is limited and reconstruction accuracy is not perfect, so analysis is based on an approximation.
future_direction: Investigate a wider range of language pairs to validate and extend the observations.
Combine sparse autoencoders with other analytical methods for a more robust understanding.
papers.abstract: This study explores how bilingual language models develop complex internal representations. We employ sparse autoencoders to analyze internal representations of bilingual language models with a focus on the effects of training steps, layers, and model sizes. Our analysis shows that language models first learn languages separately, and then gradually form bilingual alignments, particularly in the mid layers. We also found that this bilingual tendency is stronger in larger models. Building on these findings, we demonstrate the critical role of bilingual representations in model performance by employing a novel method that integrates decomposed representations from a fully trained model into a mid-training model. Our results provide insights into how language models acquire bilingual capabilities.

papers.title: Stable and Interpretable Unrolled Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can unrolled sparse coding networks be used for provable dictionary learning, addressing biased code estimates and gradient instability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PUDLE, a provable unrolled dictionary learning method with theoretical guarantees on code support recovery and gradient stability, and demonstrates interpretability.
papers.conclusion: PUDLE enables stable and interpretable dictionary learning with theoretical convergence guarantees, and outperforms existing methods in dictionary recovery and image denoising.
papers.key_findings:
Unrolled sparse coding can recover and preserve the correct code support under proper initialization and regularization.
Using reconstruction loss in backpropagation (gae-ls_t) mitigates bias propagation and leads to better dictionary recovery compared to other gradient estimates.
Proper dictionary initialization and loss choice resolve gradient instability in unrolled networks.
The unrolled network is interpretable, with mathematical relations between learned dictionary, sparse codes, and training data.
PUDLE outperforms NOODL and SPORCO in dictionary learning and image denoising tasks.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis relies on assumptions like finite-iteration support selection and strong convexity, which may be stringent for generalization beyond dictionary learning.
The analysis is conducted in the noiseless setting; extension to noisy measurements is left for future work.
future_direction: Generalize the analysis to other min-min optimization problems like ridge regression and logistic regression.
Extend the analysis to noisy settings.
Derive finite-sample bounds for dictionary learning with unrolled networks.
papers.abstract: The dictionary learning problem, representing data as a combination of a few atoms, has long stood as a popular method for learning representations in statistics and signal processing. The most popular dictionary learning algorithm alternates between sparse coding and dictionary update steps, and a rich literature has studied its theoretical convergence. The success of dictionary learning relies on access to a "good" initial estimate of the dictionary and the ability of the sparse coding step to provide an unbiased estimate of the code. The growing popularity of unrolled sparse coding networks has led to the empirical finding that backpropagation through such networks performs dictionary learning. We offer the theoretical analysis of these empirical results through PUDLE, a Provable Unrolled Dictionary LEarning method. We provide conditions on the network initialization and data distribution sufficient to recover and preserve the support of the latent code. Additionally, we address two challenges; first, the vanilla unrolled sparse coding computes a biased code estimate, and second, gradients during backpropagated learning can become unstable. We show approaches to reduce the bias of the code estimate in the forward pass, and that of the dictionary estimate in the backward pass. We propose strategies to resolve the learning instability by tuning network parameters and modifying the loss function. Overall, we highlight the impact of loss, unrolling, and backpropagation on convergence. We complement our findings through synthetic and image denoising experiments. Finally, we demonstrate PUDLE's interpretability, a driving factor in designing deep networks based on iterative optimizations, by building a mathematical relation between network weights, its output, and the training set.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Generalize? A Case Study of Answerability
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders capture abstract concepts like answerability in a way that generalizes across diverse datasets?
papers.core_contribution: SAE features for answerability show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, sometimes generalizing well and sometimes poorly, indicating the need for better evaluation methods for SAE-based interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Comprehensive out-of-distribution evaluation is critical for SAE-based interpretability, as SAE features show inconsistent generalization, highlighting the need for better evaluation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains for answerability detection.
SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, with performance varying from near-random to better than residual stream probes.
Standard SAE feature search can fail to identify generalizing features even when they exist.
Linear probes on the residual stream also exhibit high variance in generalization across datasets.
Combining multiple SAE features does not improve out-of-domain performance over the best single feature.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to Gemma 2 due to lack of high-quality SAEs for other instruction-tuned LLMs.
SAE features depend on training hyperparameters and data, affecting generalizability.
Simple SAE probe training techniques were used, which may not yield optimal results.
Feature splitting in SAEs may cause abstract concepts like answerability to be split into many separate features, complicating detection.
future_direction: Developing better evaluation methods for SAE feature generalization.
Improving SAE training methods to encourage learning of general features.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach in language model interpretability, offering unsupervised extraction of sparse features. For interpretability methods to succeed, they must identify abstract features across domains, and these features can often manifest differently in each context. We examine this through "answerability" - a model's ability to recognize answerable questions. We extensively evaluate SAE feature generalization across diverse, partly self-constructed answerability datasets for Gemma 2 SAEs. Our analysis reveals that residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains, but generalization performance differs sharply. SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain transfer, with performance varying from almost random to outperforming residual stream probes. Overall, this demonstrates the need for robust evaluation methods and quantitative approaches to predict feature generalization in SAE-based interpretability.

papers.title: Exploring Task Performance with Interpretable Models via Sparse Auto-Encoders
papers.research_question: We investigated the extent to which the decomposition of traditionally black-box LLMs can aid in increasing their interpretability and lead to performance improvements in downstream tasks such as mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to decompose LLMs, identify model-internal misunderstandings, and automatically reformulate prompts to improve performance on downstream tasks like mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection.
papers.conclusion: Decomposing LLMs with dictionary learning and sparse autoencoders improves interpretability and leads to performance gains in mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection by identifying and correcting model-internal misunderstandings.
papers.key_findings:
Decomposing LLMs with sparse autoencoders allows identification of ambiguous mathematical symbols and metaphorical terms.
Automatic reformulation of prompts based on identified ambiguities improves accuracy in mathematical reasoning across multiple models and domains.
The method also improves metaphor detection accuracy, outperforming previous task-specific models.
The improvements are statistically significant, as shown by paired t-tests.
The framework is model-agnostic and works across different LLMs (Llama 3, Mistral, Gemma, Phi-3).
papers.limitation:
The work does not introduce a new interpretability technique but applies existing techniques in a novel framework.
The approach is only tested on two downstream tasks (mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection), and performance on other tasks may vary.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are traditionally viewed as black-box algorithms, therefore reducing trustworthiness and obscuring potential approaches to increasing performance on downstream tasks. In this work, we apply an effective LLM decomposition method using a dictionary-learning approach with sparse autoencoders. This helps extract monosemantic features from polysemantic LLM neurons. Remarkably, our work identifies model-internal misunderstanding, allowing the automatic reformulation of the prompts with additional annotations to improve the interpretation by LLMs. Moreover, this approach demonstrates a significant performance improvement in downstream tasks, such as mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection.

papers.title: Binary Autoencoder for Mechanistic Interpretability of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to enforce global sparsity and feature independence in autoencoders for LLM interpretability to avoid dense features and improve feature atomization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Binary Autoencoder (BAE), an autoencoder variant with binarized hidden activations and entropy constraints, to improve global sparsity and feature atomization in LLM interpretability, enabling efficient entropy estimation and extraction of interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: BAE provides a novel approach for mechanistic interpretability by enabling entropy-based analysis and sparse feature extraction, advancing the understanding of LLM internal dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
BAE enables accurate entropy estimation on hidden state sets, revealing layer bandwidth and implicit context windows in LLMs.
BAE suppresses dense features and extracts the largest number of interpretable features compared to baselines.
In-context learning is interpreted as a form of information reduction, where more demonstrations lead to lower entropy.
BAE's training objective promotes feature independence and sparsity across instances.
The proposed ComSem method improves feature interpretation by avoiding numerical reasoning in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending BAE to more layers and models
Investigating theoretical foundations
Applying to multimodal settings
papers.abstract: Existing works are dedicated to untangling atomized numerical components (features) from the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, they typically rely on autoencoders constrained by some training-time regularization on single training instances, without an explicit guarantee of global sparsity among instances, causing a large amount of dense (simultaneously inactive) features, harming the feature sparsity and atomization. In this paper, we propose a novel autoencoder variant that enforces minimal entropy on minibatches of hidden activations, thereby promoting feature independence and sparsity across instances. For efficient entropy calculation, we discretize the hidden activations to 1-bit via a step function and apply gradient estimation to enable backpropagation, so that we term it as Binary Autoencoder (BAE) and empirically demonstrate two major applications: (1) Feature set entropy calculation. Entropy can be reliably estimated on binary hidden activations, which can be leveraged to characterize the inference dynamics of LLMs. (2) Feature untangling. Compared to typical methods, due to improved training strategy, BAE avoids dense features while producing the largest number of interpretable ones among baselines.

papers.title: Number Representations in LLMs: A Computational Parallel to Human Perception
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) encode numerical values in a logarithmic-like structure, similar to the human mental number line hypothesis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode numerical values with structured, sublinear compression akin to the human logarithmic mental number line, a pattern detectable via unsupervised methods like PCA but often obscured by supervised linear probes like PLS.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode numerical values with structured compression similar to the human mental number line, but this sublinearity is only detectable through unsupervised dimensionality reduction methods like PCA that preserve geometric relationships.
papers.key_findings:
Numerical embeddings in LLMs exhibit higher explained variance and stronger monotonicity compared to random letter sequences, indicating a structured number line.
The Scaling Rate Index (β) reveals sublinear scaling (β < 1) in many models, showing compression where distances between numbers decrease as values increase.
PCA captures the underlying sublinear structure of numerical representations, while PLS, as a supervised linear probe, often misses this non-uniformity by optimizing for covariance with the target.
Layer-wise analysis shows that the sublinear encoding is consistent across layers, with the layer of highest explained variance also showing strong monotonicity.
In real-world tasks, birth year data shows systematic sublinear encoding, while population data is less structured due to context-dependence and approximate expressions.
papers.abstract: Humans are believed to perceive numbers on a logarithmic mental number line, where smaller values are represented with greater resolution than larger ones. This cognitive bias, supported by neuroscience and behavioral studies, suggests that numerical magnitudes are processed in a sublinear fashion rather than on a uniform linear scale. Inspired by this hypothesis, we investigate whether large language models (LLMs) exhibit a similar logarithmic-like structure in their internal numerical representations. By analyzing how numerical values are encoded across different layers of LLMs, we apply dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA and PLS followed by geometric regression to uncover latent structures in the learned embeddings. Our findings reveal that the model's numerical representations exhibit sublinear spacing, with distances between values aligning with a logarithmic scale. This suggests that LLMs, much like humans, may encode numbers in a compressed, non-uniform manner.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to, given that neurons are multifaceted?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron and improves activation maximization image quality with more natural colors and coherent global structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization and provides a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function by revealing its multiple facets.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level neurons.
The MFV algorithm produces visualizations with more natural colors and coherent global structure by separately synthesizing each facet.
The algorithm reveals that DNNs learn global structure, details, and context of objects, acting more like generative models.
A center-biased regularization technique reduces the repetition of object fragments in activation maximization images.
papers.limitation:
The number of unique images MFV produces for a unit depends on the manually set k in k-means; automatically identifying the true number of facets remains an open question.
It is unclear whether hidden fully connected layer neurons are truly amalgams of different concepts or part of distributed representations; current visualization methods (Deconv, LRP) do not conclusively reveal this.
future_direction: Future research is needed to understand the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves activation maximization quality.
Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron is an important open scientific question.
Further investigation into the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons and whether they are amalgams or represent abstract concepts.
papers.abstract: We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted, in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example, a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc. Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each neuron.

papers.title: Switched linear encoding with rectified linear autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the coding behavior of autoencoders with rectified linear activations, and how do they relate to other sparse linear coding models?
papers.core_contribution: Unifies sparse linear coding models through analysis of rectified linear autoencoders and provides an intuitive geometric interpretation of their behavior.
papers.conclusion: Synthesizes recent work on encoding and provides an intuitive interpretation of rectified linear autoencoders, emphasizing the importance of whitening.
papers.key_findings:
Rectified linear autoencoders unify sparse coding models and behave like mixtures of exponentially many linear or ICA models, selecting one per input.
They produce sparse activations with true zeros, effectively deactivating irrelevant features for each input.
Feature vectors often pair as negated images, particularly in overcomplete dictionaries, splitting data into orthants.
Whitening input data is crucial for the performance of switched-linear coding models like rectified linear autoencoders.
Visualizations on artificial and MNIST data show that learned features align with data axes and capture stroke-like structures in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Sigmoid activation functions saturate for points far from the hyperplane, limiting discrimination ability.
Linear activations are unbounded, leading to numerical instability during training with large-scale inputs.
The connection between whitening and linear autoencoders is poorly understood and requires further exploration.
future_direction: Further exploration of whitening, particularly whitening local regions of the input space.
papers.abstract: Several recent results in machine learning have established formal connections between autoencoders---artificial neural network models that attempt to reproduce their inputs---and other coding models like sparse coding and K-means. This paper explores in depth an autoencoder model that is constructed using rectified linear activations on its hidden units. Our analysis builds on recent results to further unify the world of sparse linear coding models. We provide an intuitive interpretation of the behavior of these coding models and demonstrate this intuition using small, artificial datasets with known distributions.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: I Predict Therefore I Am: Is Next Token Prediction Enough to Learn Human-Interpretable Concepts from Data?
papers.research_question: Is next-token prediction sufficient for large language models to learn human-interpretable concepts from data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes that LLM representations learned via next-token prediction are approximately a linear transformation of the log-posterior of latent human-interpretable concepts, providing a theoretical foundation for the linear representation hypothesis and motivating a principled evaluation method for sparse autoencoders.
papers.conclusion: Next-token prediction enables LLMs to learn human-interpretable concepts, and the linear identifiability result offers a unified perspective on the linear representation hypothesis and a principled approach for evaluating concept disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Under mild conditions, LLM representations are approximately a linear transformation of the log-posterior of latent concepts.
This linear property provides a unified explanation for empirical phenomena like concepts as directions and linear probing.
The linear property motivates a principled evaluation method for sparse autoencoders using linear probes.
Structured SAEs, which incorporate low-rank regularization, improve concept disentanglement compared to standard SAEs.
Empirical validation on simulation data and multiple LLM families (Pythia, Llama, DeepSeek) supports the theoretical results.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis relies on assumptions such as the diversity condition and approximate invertibility, which may not hold in all scenarios.
The evaluation of sparse autoencoders depends on the quality of linear probes, which may be noisy.
future_direction: Rethinking invertibility assumptions in causal representation learning.
Embedding causal reasoning in LLMs through linear unmixing.
papers.abstract: The remarkable achievements of large language models (LLMs) have led many to conclude that they exhibit a form of intelligence. This is as opposed to explanations of their capabilities based on their ability to perform relatively simple manipulations of vast volumes of data. To illuminate the distinction between these explanations, we introduce a novel generative model that generates tokens on the basis of human-interpretable concepts represented as latent discrete variables. Under mild conditions, even when the mapping from the latent space to the observed space is non-invertible, we establish an identifiability result, i.e., the representations learned by LLMs through next-token prediction can be approximately modeled as the logarithm of the posterior probabilities of these latent discrete concepts given input context, up to an invertible linear transformation. This theoretical finding not only provides evidence that LLMs capture underlying generative factors, but also provide a unified prospective for understanding of the linear representation hypothesis. Taking this a step further, our finding motivates a reliable evaluation of sparse autoencoders by treating the performance of supervised concept extractors as an upper bound. Pushing this idea even further, it inspires a structural variant that enforces dependence among latent concepts in addition to promoting sparsity. Empirically, we validate our theoretical results through evaluations on both simulation data and the Pythia, Llama, and DeepSeek model families, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our structured sparse autoencoder.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Sparse Coding and Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether gradient descent on the squared loss of an autoencoder can solve the dictionary learning problem.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that for a single-layer ReLU autoencoder, the expected gradient of the squared loss is asymptotically negligible near the true dictionary A*, suggesting that A* is a critical point, and shows that the ReLU layer can recover the support of sparse codes.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that the expected gradient of the squared loss is very close to zero near the generating dictionary, suggesting that sparse coding can be solved by training autoencoders with gradient descent.
papers.key_findings:
A layer of ReLU gates can recover the support of the sparse code when the weight matrix is close to the dictionary.
The expected gradient of the squared loss function is asymptotically negligible in a neighborhood of the true dictionary A*.
Experimental results show that the gradient norm is of order h^{p-1} and decreases with the sparse code dimension h.
Experiments suggest that A* is a local minimum of the squared loss function.
The results provide evidence that sparse coding problems can be tackled by training autoencoders.
papers.limitation:
It remains to show whether gradient descent with random initialization converges to the neighborhood of A*.
The analysis applies to the expected gradient; sample complexity is not analyzed.
Efficient implementations of the iterative update rule based on the exact gradient are left for future work.
future_direction: Rigorous analysis of gradient descent convergence from random initialization.
Analysis of sample complexity for the gradient results.
Extending the analysis to deeper autoencoder architectures.
papers.abstract: In this work we study the landscape of squared loss of an Autoencoder when the data generative model is that of “Sparse Coding”/“Dictionary Learning”. The neural net considered is an <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n}$</tex> mapping and has a single ReLU activation layer of size <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$h > n$</tex> . The net has access to vectors <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$y\in \mathbb{R}^{n}$</tex> obtained as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$y=A^{\ast}x^{\ast}$</tex> where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$x^{\ast}\in \mathbb{R}^{h}$</tex> are sparse high dimensional vectors and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A^{\ast}\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times h}$</tex> is an overcomplete incoherent matrix. Under very mild distributional assumptions on <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$x^{\ast}$</tex> , we prove that the norm of the expected gradient of the squared loss function is asymptotically (in sparse code dimension) negligible for all points in a small neighborhood of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A^{\ast}$</tex> . This is supported with experimental evidence using synthetic data. We conduct experiments to suggest that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A^{\ast}$</tex> sits at the bottom of a well in the landscape and we also give experiments showing that gradient descent on this loss function gets columnwise very close to the original dictionary even with far enough initialization. Along the way we prove that a layer of ReLU gates can be set up to automatically recover the support of the sparse codes. Since this property holds independent of the loss function we believe that it could be of independent interest. A full version of this paper is accessible at: https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.03735

papers.title: Decomposing multimodal embedding spaces with group-sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to adapt sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for multimodal embeddings to mitigate the tradeoff between monosemanticity and modality alignment.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a group-sparse autoencoder with cross-modal random masking to learn multimodal dictionaries from aligned embeddings, improving modality alignment, reducing dead neurons, and enhancing feature semanticity compared to standard SAEs.
papers.conclusion: The proposed group-sparse autoencoder with cross-modal random masking learns dictionaries with better multimodal alignment, fewer dead neurons, and improved semanticity, enabling better interpretability and control in cross-modal tasks.
papers.key_findings:
MGSAE increases the number of neurons that activate for both modalities and reduces dead neurons.
MGSAE improves multimodal monosemanticity scores compared to standard SAEs.
MGSAE improves zero-shot performance on cross-modal tasks like image/text and audio/text classification and retrieval.
The method enables better interpretability, e.g., in concept naming for linear probes on attributes like 'blonde hair'.
The approach generalizes to different multimodal encoders (SIGLIP2, AIMv2) and datasets (MS COCO).
papers.abstract: The Linear Representation Hypothesis asserts that the embeddings learned by neural networks can be understood as linear combinations of features corresponding to high-level concepts.
