Additionally, intervention experiments using 2x2 factorial stimulus designs demonstrated that integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce systematic behavioral effects on model outputs, including significant statistical interaction effects across semantic dimensions. This work provides systematic evidence for (1) dual encoding in neural representations, (2) meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature interactions, and (3) introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of\n Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple types of features (facets) each neuron responds to, and improves activation maximization visualizations with more natural colors and coherent structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization by producing higher quality images and shows the multiple feature facets each neuron detects, providing a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level ones.
Multifaceted feature visualization produces more realistic and interpretable visualizations than previous activation maximization methods.
The method reveals that DNNs learn not only discriminative features but also global structure and context, similar to generative models.
Hidden fully connected layer neurons sometimes represent amalgams of different concepts.
papers.limitation:
The number of facets visualized depends on the manually set parameter k in k-means; automatically determining the true number of facets remains an open problem.
The method does not always reconstruct a proper facet (e.g., for stuffed peppers), possibly because the neuron ignores certain features.
Center-biased regularization is not guaranteed to produce a single object; it only biases optimization toward the center.
future_direction: Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron.
Investigating the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves visualization quality.
Further research into understanding the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons.
papers.abstract:
We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features
each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have
created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which
synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each
neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron
detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted,
in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example,
a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a
storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images
without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating
inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc.
Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of
each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of
images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that
produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images
obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of
image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate
colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus
provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each
neuron.

papers.title: Evaluating Open-Source Sparse Autoencoders on Disentangling Factual Knowledge in GPT-2 Small
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature spaces are useful for causal interpretability analysis, specifically for disentangling related factual knowledge (country and continent of cities) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: Current open-source sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for GPT-2 small struggle to provide a feature space that better disentangles factual knowledge than the baseline of neurons, and none approach the performance of the supervised DAS skyline.
papers.conclusion: Only one of the evaluated SAEs reached the neuron baseline and none reached the DAS skyline, indicating current SAEs are not superior to neurons for this causal disentanglement task, but the evaluation is a useful step for assessing SAEs in interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Using representations reconstructed by SAEs degrades the model's knowledge of cities.
The end-to-end SAEs degrade knowledge less relative to their reconstruction loss, but this is weak evidence.
There is a significant gap between the neuron baseline and the DAS skyline, showing neurons can be improved upon.
Current SAEs for GPT-2 small generally perform below the neuron baseline, with only the top-k Open AI SAE matching it.
The top-k SAE (Open AI SAE) is the most performant among the evaluated SAEs.
papers.limitation: The evaluation is limited to GPT-2 small and a specific dataset (cities, countries, continents). Future work should scale to larger models and more attributes.
future_direction: Scale experiments to models with available SAEs including gemma, Mistral, Llama, and Pythia.
Use more attributes from the RA VEL dataset, such as language, gender, etc., for larger models with more knowledge.
papers.abstract: A popular new method in mechanistic interpretability is to train high-dimensional sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on neuron activations and use SAE features as the atomic units of analysis. However, the body of evidence on whether SAE feature spaces are useful for causal analysis is underdeveloped. In this work, we use the RAVEL benchmark to evaluate whether SAEs trained on hidden representations of GPT-2 small have sets of features that separately mediate knowledge of which country a city is in and which continent it is in. We evaluate four open-source SAEs for GPT-2 small against each other, with neurons serving as a baseline, and linear features learned via distributed alignment search (DAS) serving as a skyline. For each, we learn a binary mask to select features that will be patched to change the country of a city without changing the continent, or vice versa. Our results show that SAEs struggle to reach the neuron baseline, and none come close to the DAS skyline. We release code here: https://github.com/MaheepChaudhary/SAE-Ravel

papers.title: Visual Exploration of Feature Relationships in Sparse Autoencoders with Curated Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we enable effective, focused exploration of the relationships between sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and human-interpretable concepts in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a focused exploration framework and an interactive visualization system (SAE Semantic Explorer) that integrates topology-based visual encodings with dimensionality reduction to enable targeted analysis of relationships between SAE features and curated concepts.
papers.conclusion: The proposed visualization framework provides a scalable and interpretable means of exploring how user-defined concepts relate to the structured knowledge encoded in SAEs across layers, facilitating deeper insight into model organization.
papers.key_findings:
The framework reveals that concept relationships evolve across model layers, with early layers showing dense clustering, middle layers showing separation and specialization, and deeper layers showing more integrated structures.
The ball mapper view provides a complementary perspective to UMAP, preserving local neighborhood relationships and revealing structural distortions introduced by dimensionality reduction.
The tool enables the discovery of semantic boundaries and transitions between related concepts, such as tracing a path from 'Computer Science' to 'Mathematics' in the feature space.
papers.limitation: The reliability of identified features depends heavily on the quality of their automatically generated explanations (auto-interpretability).
future_direction: Enhance the UMAP visualization by integrating scalable and annotated visualization toolkits.
Leverage LLMs to automatically generate richer, context-aware explanations for mapper nodes.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for uncovering interpretable features in large language models (LLMs) through the sparse directions they learn. However, the sheer number of extracted directions makes comprehensive exploration intractable. While conventional embedding techniques such as UMAP can reveal global structure, they suffer from limitations including high-dimensional compression artifacts, overplotting, and misleading neighborhood distortions. In this work, we propose a focused exploration framework that prioritizes curated concepts and their corresponding SAE features over attempts to visualize all available features simultaneously. We present an interactive visualization system that combines topology-based visual encoding with dimensionality reduction to faithfully represent both local and global relationships among selected features. This hybrid approach enables users to investigate SAE behavior through targeted, interpretable subsets, facilitating deeper and more nuanced analysis of concept representation in latent space.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Which Sparse Autoencoder Features Are Real? Model-X Knockoffs for False Discovery Rate Control
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish real computational patterns from erroneous correlations in sparse autoencoder features? The paper investigates using Model-X knockoffs for false discovery rate control in SAE feature selection.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model-X knockoffs for selecting sparse autoencoder features with false discovery rate control, revealing that only 25% of highly active SAE features encode genuine task-relevant information.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a rigorous statistical framework for identifying genuine SAE features with FDR control, addressing a critical gap in interpretability research and showing that naive feature analysis approaches are dominated by false positives.
papers.key_findings:
The method selected 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 from 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification.
Selected features show a 5.40× separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features.
Only about 25% of the examined latents carry task-relevant signal, while 75% do not.
A classifier using only the selected features achieved 77.4% training accuracy.
Features with negative knockoff statistics exist, indicating misleading patterns that would be selected by naive correlation-based approaches.
papers.limitation:
Feature reduction is necessary for stable covariance estimation (n > p), which may miss rare but important features.
Computational cost scales quadratically in p, becoming expensive for very large feature sets.
The method identifies which features are real but does not explain what those features represent.
The method identifies statistical association, not necessarily causal importance.
future_direction: Explore hierarchical testing strategies, approximate knockoff methods, or alternative covariance estimation techniques to handle p ≫ n settings.
Combine knockoff-based selection with automated interpretation pipelines to provide both statistical validation and conceptual understanding.
Investigate how feature validity varies across layers and tasks, and how selection interacts with different SAE training objectives and architectures.
papers.abstract: Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are crucial for identifying interpretable features in neural networks, it is still challenging to distinguish between real computational patterns and erroneous correlations. We introduce Model-X knockoffs to SAE feature selection, using knock-off+ to control the false discovery rate (FDR) with finite-sample guarantees under the standard Model-X assumptions (in our case, via a Gaussian surrogate for the latent distribution). We select 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 after analyzing 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification using Pythia-70M. About 25% of the latents under examination carry task-relevant signal, whereas 75% do not, according to the chosen set, which displays a 5.40x separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features. Our method offers a re-producible and principled framework for reliable feature discovery by combining SAEs with multiple-testing-aware inference, advancing the foundations of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Jumping Ahead: Improving Reconstruction Fidelity with JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the reconstruction fidelity of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) at a given sparsity level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces JumpReLU SAEs, a simple modification of ReLU SAEs that achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level and is similarly interpretable to other SAE methods.
papers.conclusion: JumpReLU SAEs are a mild improvement over prevailing SAE training methodologies, offering better or equal reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity, similar interpretability, and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
JumpReLU SAEs consistently provide more faithful reconstructions than Gated SAEs and at least as good as, and often slightly better than, TopK SAEs at a given sparsity level.
JumpReLU SAEs have few dead features without the need for resampling during training.
JumpReLU SAEs have a similar proportion of very high frequency features (active on >10% of tokens) as TopK SAEs, which is higher than Gated SAEs.
Manual and automated interpretability studies show that JumpReLU SAE features are similarly interpretable to Gated and TopK SAE features.
JumpReLU SAEs are efficient to train, requiring no auxiliary loss terms and having an elementwise activation function (unlike TopK).
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are conducted on a single model (Gemma 2 9B), raising uncertainty about transfer to other models.
The science of principled evaluations of SAE performance is still in its infancy; it is unclear how well current metrics correlate with downstream utility.
JumpReLU SAEs tend to have relatively more very high frequency features than Gated SAEs.
JumpReLU SAEs introduce new hyperparameters (initial threshold and bandwidth) that require selection.
future_direction: Evaluate SAEs on a broader selection of metrics that more directly correspond to the value SAEs add by aiding or enabling downstream tasks, such as circuit analysis or model control.
Further tweak the loss function used to train JumpReLU SAEs to directly tackle the phenomenon of high frequency features.
Develop more principled ways to choose hyperparameters, such as the bandwidth parameter, possibly borrowing from kernel density estimation literature.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising unsupervised approach for identifying causally relevant and interpretable linear features in a language model's (LM) activations. To be useful for downstream tasks, SAEs need to decompose LM activations faithfully; yet to be interpretable the decomposition must be sparse -- two objectives that are in tension. In this paper, we introduce JumpReLU SAEs, which achieve state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level on Gemma 2 9B activations, compared to other recent advances such as Gated and TopK SAEs. We also show that this improvement does not come at the cost of interpretability through manual and automated interpretability studies. JumpReLU SAEs are a simple modification of vanilla (ReLU) SAEs -- where we replace the ReLU with a discontinuous JumpReLU activation function -- and are similarly efficient to train and run. By utilising straight-through-estimators (STEs) in a principled manner, we show how it is possible to train JumpReLU SAEs effectively despite the discontinuous JumpReLU function introduced in the SAE's forward pass. Similarly, we use STEs to directly train L0 to be sparse, instead of training on proxies such as L1, avoiding problems like shrinkage.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Tokenized SAEs: Disentangling SAE Reconstructions
papers.research_question: How tightly do SAE features correspond to computationally important directions in language models, and how does training data imbalance cause SAEs to learn token reconstruction features?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Tokenized SAEs, which use a per-token bias to separate token reconstruction from feature reconstruction, leading to more semantically meaningful features and improved reconstruction in sparse regimes.
papers.conclusion: Tokenized SAEs effectively disentangle token reconstruction from feature reconstruction, mitigating the bias toward common n-grams and enabling the learning of more interesting, semantically useful features.
papers.key_findings:
Many SAE features predominantly correspond to simple input statistics (n-grams) due to training data class imbalance and lack of complex error signals.
Tokenized SAEs outperform non-tokenized SAEs in reconstruction quality and sparsity, achieving the same reconstruction with about 25% sparsity.
Tokenized SAEs learn features that are more semantically meaningful and complex, with fewer features activated by individual unigrams.
Tokenized SAEs train significantly faster, reaching baseline performance 6-10x faster across layers of GPT-2.
The method scales to larger models like Pythia 1.4B, where it still outperforms baseline SAEs.
papers.limitation: The qualitative evaluation of feature complexity and consistency is based on a limited sample size and should be interpreted cautiously as preliminary indications.
future_direction: Incorporating n-gram statistics instead of simply unigrams in the lookup table.
A more thorough study into the quality of Tokenized SAE features, both in the dictionary and the lookup table.
Characterizing token reconstruction similarity in latent representations.
papers.abstract: Sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) have become a prevalent tool for interpreting language models' inner workings. However, it is unknown how tightly SAE features correspond to computationally important directions in the model. This work empirically shows that many RES-JB SAE features predominantly correspond to simple input statistics. We hypothesize this is caused by a large class imbalance in training data combined with a lack of complex error signals. To reduce this behavior, we propose a method that disentangles token reconstruction from feature reconstruction. This improvement is achieved by introducing a per-token bias, which provides an enhanced baseline for interesting reconstruction. As a result, significantly more interesting features and improved reconstruction in sparse regimes are learned.

papers.title: TopK Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we build a language model architecture that enjoys the interpretability of sparse autoencoders without suffering the drawbacks of post-hoc training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TopK LMs, a transformer-based language model architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function to achieve inherent, SAE-like interpretability without requiring post-hoc training, while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: TopK LMs represent a significant advance toward trustworthy AI systems by making interpretability a built-in feature, demonstrating that performance and interpretability need not be competing objectives.
papers.key_findings:
TopK LMs achieve competitive language modeling and downstream task performance compared to dense baselines, with only a moderate increase in model size.
Neurons in TopK LMs exhibit higher concept specialization, as measured by lower token and semantic entropy, making them more interpretable.
Single-neuron interventions (activation patching) can causally steer the model's text generation towards specific concepts.
The formation and specialization of individual neurons can be traced continuously across training checkpoints and model layers.
Sparsity annealing during training improves convergence and model performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models up to ~1B parameters; effectiveness on significantly larger models remains an open question.
Evaluation focused on language modeling and standard reasoning benchmarks, leaving performance on specialized downstream tasks unclear.
Long-context modeling capabilities and the interaction between TopK sparsity and attention over long sequences were not examined.
The approach is currently limited to text-only models; extending to multimodal architectures requires future research.
Specific societal applications that could benefit from the model's interpretability were not explored.
future_direction: Scaling the TopK LM approach to significantly larger models (tens or hundreds of billions of parameters).
Extending TopK activation to multimodal architectures combining text with images, audio, or other modalities.
Investigating how TopK LMs can address concrete challenges in model alignment, fairness assessment, safety evaluation, and trustworthy AI deployment.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an important tool for analyzing and interpreting the activation space of transformer-based language models (LMs). However, SAEs suffer several shortcomings that diminish their utility and internal validity. Since SAEs are trained post-hoc, it is unclear if the failure to discover a particular concept is a failure on the SAE's side or due to the underlying LM not representing this concept. This problem is exacerbated by training conditions and architecture choices affecting which features an SAE learns. When tracing how LMs learn concepts during training, the lack of feature stability also makes it difficult to compare SAEs features across different checkpoints. To address these limitations, we introduce a modification to the transformer architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function at chosen layers, making the model's hidden states equivalent to the latent features of a TopK SAE. This approach eliminates the need for post-hoc training while providing interpretability comparable to SAEs. The resulting TopK LMs offer a favorable trade-off between model size, computational efficiency, and interpretability. Despite this simple architectural change, TopK LMs maintain their original capabilities while providing robust interpretability benefits. Our experiments demonstrate that the sparse representations learned by TopK LMs enable successful steering through targeted neuron interventions and facilitate detailed analysis of neuron formation processes across checkpoints and layers. These features make TopK LMs stable and reliable tools for understanding how language models learn and represent concepts, which we believe will significantly advance future research on model interpretability and controllability.

papers.title: Exploring Internal Numeracy in Language Models: A Case Study on ALBERT
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models internally represent numerical data, such as numerals and their textual counterparts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that ALBERT models internally represent numerical concepts in a structured way, with embeddings ordered by value along principal components, suggesting logarithmic scaling.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that ALBERT models internally encode numerical ordering in their embeddings, with evidence of logarithmic scaling, providing insights into model numeracy.
papers.key_findings:
ALBERT models use primary PCA axes to represent ordering of numbers, ordinals, and magnitude orders.
Representations are closer for higher values, indicating a logarithmic scale.
Numerals and textual counterparts form separate clusters but increase along the same direction in PCA space.
Orders of magnitude words are ordered correctly along the first PCA axis.
Ordinal terms are represented in correct order up to 'seventh', with decreasing separation for higher values.
papers.limitation: Focus on single-token numbers excludes decimals and larger numerical values.
future_direction: Quantify to what extent learned internal structures reflect interval and ratio scales.
Investigate contributions of model architecture and term frequency in the corpus.
Extend analysis to multi-token numbers and mathematical operators.
papers.abstract: It has been found that Transformer-based language models have the ability to perform basic quantitative reasoning. In this paper, we propose a method for studying how these models internally represent numerical data, and use our proposal to analyze the ALBERT family of language models. Specifically, we extract the learned embeddings these models use to represent tokens that correspond to numbers and ordinals, and subject these embeddings to Principal Component Analysis (PCA). PCA results reveal that ALBERT models of different sizes, trained and initialized separately, consistently learn to use the axes of greatest variation to represent the approximate ordering of various numerical concepts. Numerals and their textual counterparts are represented in separate clusters, but increase along the same direction in 2D space. Our findings illustrate that language models, trained purely to model text, can intuit basic mathematical concepts, opening avenues for NLP applications that intersect with quantitative reasoning.

papers.title: The Origins of Representation Manifolds in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are features represented as manifolds in large language models, and how does cosine similarity in representation space relate to the intrinsic geometry of features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical framework to explain representation manifolds in LLMs, showing that under the continuous correspondence hypothesis, cosine similarity encodes the intrinsic geometry of features through shortest paths on the manifold, and validates this on text embeddings and token activations.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a formal mathematical framework to explain and interpret representation manifolds in large language models, validating the theory on internal representations and text embeddings, and revealing unexpected encodings of distances.
papers.key_findings:
Representation manifolds in LLMs reflect the topology of features (e.g., colors and dates form loops, years form a curve) as predicted by the continuous correspondence hypothesis.
Cosine similarity between feature representations locally reflects distance in the feature metric space, implying isometry up to scaling.
Years in GPT2-small are encoded on a logarithmic scale rather than linear, with larger distances between more recent years.
For colors in text-embedding-large-3, the representations follow a hue cycle rather than other possible encodings like RGB.
The manifold geometry allows linear computation of functions of the feature value, supporting the superposition hypothesis.
papers.limitation:
The hypothesis-driven approach is manual and not scalable, relying on a reasonable starting hypothesis for the metric space.
PCA may not capture the full complexity of distances encoded by the language model, which might be more complex and not correspond to human understanding.
Estimating manifolds in the presence of noise is statistically difficult, and the K-nearest-neighbour graph approach is prone to short-circuits causing errors.
future_direction: Learning the metric automatically rather than manual hypothesis
Developing 'manifold-aware' sparse autoencoders
Using the metric space formalism in future scientific discourse
papers.abstract: There is a large ongoing scientific effort in mechanistic interpretability to map embeddings and internal representations of AI systems into human-understandable concepts. A key element of this effort is the linear representation hypothesis, which posits that neural representations are sparse linear combinations of `almost-orthogonal' direction vectors, reflecting the presence or absence of different features. This model underpins the use of sparse autoencoders to recover features from representations. Moving towards a fuller model of features, in which neural representations could encode not just the presence but also a potentially continuous and multidimensional value for a feature, has been a subject of intense recent discourse. We describe why and how a feature might be represented as a manifold, demonstrating in particular that cosine similarity in representation space may encode the intrinsic geometry of a feature through shortest, on-manifold paths, potentially answering the question of how distance in representation space and relatedness in concept space could be connected. The critical assumptions and predictions of the theory are validated on text embeddings and token activations of large language models.

papers.title: Sparsity Emerges Naturally in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Does sparsity emerge naturally in neural language models during training, and how is it related to word frequency and part of speech?
papers.core_contribution: Sparsity emerges naturally in neural language models, with frequent input words associated with sparse activations and frequent target words associated with concentrated gradients, and part of speech affects gradient concentration even controlling for frequency.
papers.conclusion: Sparsity emerges naturally in neural language models, and understanding this can guide sparsity constraints for interpretability and efficiency, and explain the effectiveness of certain techniques like representation summing.
papers.key_findings:
Frequent input words are associated with concentrated or sparse activations, while frequent target words are associated with dispersed activations but concentrated gradients.
Gradients associated with function words are more concentrated than those of content words, even controlling for word frequency.
Sparsity of gradients increases with target word frequency and training time.
Activation sparsity is not correlated with target word frequency.
Input word frequency correlates with activation sparsity in lower layers, and this correlation increases later in training, possibly due to information compression.
future_direction: Developing ways to manipulate the training regime to accelerate the concentration of common words.
Incorporating concentration into the training objective as a regularizer.
Studying how sparsity emerges in models designed for specific end tasks and whether concentration is a useful measure for information compression.
papers.abstract: Concerns about interpretability, computational resources, and principled inductive priors have motivated efforts to engineer sparse neural models for NLP tasks. If sparsity is important for NLP, might well-trained neural models naturally become roughly sparse? Using the Taxi-Euclidean norm to measure sparsity, we find that frequent input words are associated with concentrated or sparse activations, while frequent target words are associated with dispersed activations but concentrated gradients. We find that gradients associated with function words are more concentrated than the gradients of content words, even controlling for word frequency.

papers.title: DB-KSVD: Scalable Alternating Optimization for Disentangling High-Dimensional Embedding Spaces
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) find strong solutions to the dictionary learning problem for disentangling transformer embeddings, or if more sophisticated optimization approaches like the proposed DB-KSVD can achieve better performance.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces DB-KSVD, a scalable dictionary learning algorithm for disentangling transformer embeddings, and shows it achieves competitive performance with sparse autoencoders on standard benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that alternating optimization algorithms can be scaled to problem sizes relevant for mechanistic interpretability of large transformer models, achieving competitive results with state-of-the-art SAE approaches on standardized metrics.
papers.key_findings:
DB-KSVD scales to millions of samples and thousands of dimensions, making it applicable to large transformer models.
DB-KSVD achieves competitive results with SAE-based approaches on the SAEBench metrics, suggesting both methods may be near theoretical limits.
Matryoshka structuring improves autointerpretability and absorption but slightly degrades loss recovered and spurious correlation removal.
DB-KSVD dictionaries tend to be coherent, especially for small sparsity, and Matryoshka structuring reduces coherence.
Initializing the dictionary with a partially known structure can significantly speed up convergence.
papers.limitation:
DB-KSVD is algorithmically more complex than SAE approaches, which makes implementation more challenging.
It is not clear whether the sample size used is sufficient or whether more scaling is needed to solve the disentanglement problem.
future_direction: Further investigation into using known structures to improve performance.
Exploring whether more scaling in sample size is needed for better disentanglement.
papers.abstract: Dictionary learning has recently emerged as a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability of large transformer models. Disentangling high-dimensional transformer embeddings, however, requires algorithms that scale to high-dimensional data with large sample sizes. Recent work has explored sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for this problem. However, SAEs use a simple linear encoder to solve the sparse encoding subproblem, which is known to be NP-hard. It is therefore interesting to understand whether this structure is sufficient to find good solutions to the dictionary learning problem or if a more sophisticated algorithm could find better solutions. In this work, we propose Double-Batch KSVD (DB-KSVD), a scalable dictionary learning algorithm that adapts the classic KSVD algorithm. DB-KSVD is informed by the rich theoretical foundations of KSVD but scales to datasets with millions of samples and thousands of dimensions. We demonstrate the efficacy of DB-KSVD by disentangling embeddings of the Gemma-2-2B model and evaluating on six metrics from the SAEBench benchmark, where we achieve competitive results when compared to established approaches based on SAEs. By matching SAE performance with an entirely different optimization approach, our results suggest that (i) SAEs do find strong solutions to the dictionary learning problem and (ii) that traditional optimization approaches can be scaled to the required problem sizes, offering a promising avenue for further research. We provide an implementation of DB-KSVD at https://github.com/RomeoV/KSVD.jl.

papers.title: BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can relaxing the top-k constraint in sparse autoencoders to a batch-level constraint, allowing a variable number of latents per sample, improve reconstruction without sacrificing average sparsity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BatchTopK SAEs, a training method that improves upon TopK SAEs by relaxing the per-sample top-k constraint to a batch-level constraint, allowing variable latents per sample and improving reconstruction without sacrificing average sparsity.
papers.conclusion: BatchTopK SAEs are an effective variant of TopK SAEs that improve reconstruction by allowing a variable number of latents per sample, and small modifications to the activation function can significantly impact SAE performance.
papers.key_findings:
BatchTopK SAEs consistently outperform TopK SAEs in reconstructing activations from GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B.
BatchTopK SAEs achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art JumpReLU SAEs on GPT-2 Small and outperform them in some settings on Gemma 2 2B.
BatchTopK allows direct specification of the average number of active latents, unlike JumpReLU SAEs which require costly hyperparameter tuning to target a specific sparsity.
BatchTopK activates a variable number of latents per sample, using few latents for simple samples (e.g., <BOS>-token) and many for complex ones.
The method uses a global threshold during inference to remove batch dependency, enabling practical use.
papers.limitation:
The paper did not directly assess the human interpretability of the latents learned by BatchTopK SAEs, though architectural similarity to TopK SAEs suggests they would remain comparably interpretable.
On Gemma 2 2B, BatchTopK only outperforms JumpReLU SAEs in terms of cross-entropy degradation in the lowest sparsity setting (k=16).
future_direction: Future work is expected to continue finding improvements that better approximate the latent structure of model activations.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting language model activations by decomposing them into sparse, interpretable features. A popular approach is the TopK SAE, that uses a fixed number of the most active latents per sample to reconstruct the model activations. We introduce BatchTopK SAEs, a training method that improves upon TopK SAEs by relaxing the top-k constraint to the batch-level, allowing for a variable number of latents to be active per sample. As a result, BatchTopK adaptively allocates more or fewer latents depending on the sample, improving reconstruction without sacrificing average sparsity. We show that BatchTopK SAEs consistently outperform TopK SAEs in reconstructing activations from GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B, and achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art JumpReLU SAEs. However, an advantage of BatchTopK is that the average number of latents can be directly specified, rather than approximately tuned through a costly hyperparameter sweep. We provide code for training and evaluating BatchTopK SAEs at https://github.com/bartbussmann/BatchTopK

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture. This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: SOSAE: Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder
papers.research_question: How can the dimensionality of an autoencoder's feature space be dynamically and optimally adapted without extensive hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SOSAE, a self-organizing sparse autoencoder that uses a novel push regularization to dynamically optimize the size of feature representations during training, achieving efficient compression and feature extraction.
papers.conclusion: SOSAE effectively optimizes feature representation size via push regularization, significantly reducing computational and memory costs while maintaining model performance across various image datasets.
papers.key_findings:
SOSAE compresses input into significantly smaller feature lengths (3.1 to 4.3 times more compression) than baseline autoencoders while maintaining or improving classification accuracy.
SOSAE reduces FLOPs usage by 23.3% to 32% and memory usage significantly compared to baselines, due to structured sparsity and truncation of non-active neurons.
The feature vectors generated by SOSAE are robust to truncation; removing trailing dimensions does not cause information loss, unlike other sparse autoencoder variants.
SOSAE achieves optimal hidden layer dimensionality with up to 130 times fewer FLOPs than grid search and 34 times fewer than random search for hyperparameter tuning.
SOSAE demonstrates better denoising performance and robustness against zero-masking and Gaussian noise compared to Denoising Autoencoders, while using shorter feature representations.
papers.abstract: The process of tuning the size of the hidden layers for autoencoders has the benefit of providing optimally compressed representations for the input data. However, such hyper-parameter tuning process would take a lot of computation and time effort with grid search as the default option. In this paper, we introduce the Self-Organization Regularization for Autoencoders that dynamically adapts the dimensionality of the feature space to the optimal size. Inspired by physics concepts, Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder (SOSAE) induces sparsity in feature space in a structured way that permits the truncation of the non-active part of the feature vector without any loss of information. This is done by penalizing the autoencoder based on the magnitude and the positional index of the feature vector dimensions, which during training constricts the feature space in both terms. Extensive experiments on various datasets show that our SOSAE can tune the feature space dimensionality up to 130 times lesser Floating-point Operations (FLOPs) than other baselines while maintaining the same quality of tuning and performance.

papers.title: Interpretable Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders: A Data Analysis Toolkit
papers.research_question: How can we analyze large-scale text corpora in a cost-effective and controllable way? The paper proposes using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to create interpretable embeddings for data analysis.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE embeddings, a method using sparse autoencoders to create interpretable embeddings from text, which are more cost-effective and controllable than LLM-based labeling and dense embeddings for data analysis tasks like dataset diffing, correlation discovery, clustering, and retrieval.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a versatile tool for textual data analysis, providing a cost-effective and controllable alternative to LLM-based methods and dense embeddings. The work demonstrates the value of using data to interpret models.
papers.key_findings:
SAE embeddings identify larger frequency differences between datasets at 2-8x lower cost than LLM-based methods.
SAE embeddings reliably discover unexpected correlations between concepts in text, revealing biases and artifacts.
Filtering SAE embeddings to specific concepts enables targeted clustering along axes of interest, uncovering novel groupings not found by dense embeddings.
SAE embeddings match or outperform dense embeddings on property-based retrieval tasks.
Case studies using SAE embeddings reveal model behaviors, such as Grok-4's tendency to clarify ambiguities and Tulu-3's learned trigger phrases.
papers.limitation: SAE latent descriptions can generalize poorly to unseen texts, affecting their reliability as data labelers on out-of-distribution data.
papers.abstract: Analyzing large-scale text corpora is a core challenge in machine learning, crucial for tasks like identifying undesirable model behaviors or biases in training data. Current methods often rely on costly LLM-based techniques (e.g. annotating dataset differences) or dense embedding models (e.g. for clustering), which lack control over the properties of interest. We propose using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to create SAE embeddings: representations whose dimensions map to interpretable concepts. Through four data analysis tasks, we show that SAE embeddings are more cost-effective and reliable than LLMs and more controllable than dense embeddings. Using the large hypothesis space of SAEs, we can uncover insights such as (1) semantic differences between datasets and (2) unexpected concept correlations in documents. For instance, by comparing model responses, we find that Grok-4 clarifies ambiguities more often than nine other frontier models. Relative to LLMs, SAE embeddings uncover bigger differences at 2-8x lower cost and identify biases more reliably. Additionally, SAE embeddings are controllable: by filtering concepts, we can (3) cluster documents along axes of interest and (4) outperform dense embeddings on property-based retrieval. Using SAE embeddings, we study model behavior with two case studies: investigating how OpenAI model behavior has changed over time and finding "trigger" phrases learned by Tulu-3 (Lambert et al., 2024) from its training data. These results position SAEs as a versatile tool for unstructured data analysis and highlight the neglected importance of interpreting models through their data.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Beyond Input Activations: Identifying Influential Latents by Gradient Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Do all activated latents in a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) contribute equally to the model's output, and are only latents with high causal influence effective for model steering?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes GradSAE, a method that uses output-side gradient information to identify the most causally influential latents in Sparse Autoencoders, enabling more accurate interpretation and effective steering of LLM behavior.
papers.conclusion: GradSAE effectively identifies influential latents in SAEs and enables more reliable model steering, with results generalizing across different SAEs and layers.
papers.key_findings:
Not all activated SAE latents contribute equally to the model's output; only a subset has high causal influence.
GradSAE more accurately identifies influential latents compared to a baseline that uses only input activations.
Latents selected by GradSAE are more effective for steering the model's output in a local steering task.
The performance gap between masking top and bottom influential latents is consistent across different model layers and SAEs.
Modifying non-influential (BottomK) latents has negligible impact on model output.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on SAEs trained on instruction-tuned LLMs and one fundamental capability (instruction following for question answering). Extending GradSAE to a broader range of scenarios, including pre-trained LLMs, is noted as future work.
future_direction: Extending GradSAE to a broader range of scenarios, including pre-trained LLMs.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as powerful tools for interpreting and steering the internal representations of large language models (LLMs). However, conventional approaches to analyzing SAEs typically rely solely on input-side activations, without considering the causal influence between each latent feature and the model's output. This work is built on two key hypotheses: (1) activated latents do not contribute equally to the construction of the model's output, and (2) only latents with high causal influence are effective for model steering. To validate these hypotheses, we propose Gradient Sparse Autoencoder (GradSAE), a simple yet effective method that identifies the most influential latents by incorporating output-side gradient information.

papers.title: Priors in Time: Missing Inductive Biases for Language Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the temporal prior assumptions of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and how do they conflict with the actual temporal structure in language model activations? How can we design an interpretability method that incorporates appropriate temporal inductive biases?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Feature Analysis, a new interpretability protocol that decomposes language model activations into predictable (contextual) and novel (residual) components, capturing temporal structure that standard Sparse Autoencoders miss due to inappropriate inductive biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability tools must incorporate inductive biases that match the data's structure, and Temporal Feature Analysis offers a promising direction for capturing temporal dynamics in language model representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs impose an i.i.d. prior over time, assuming concepts are independent across time, which conflicts with the non-stationary temporal structure (e.g., increasing intrinsic dimensionality, context correlations) observed in language model activations.
Temporal Feature Analysis successfully decomposes activations into predictable (slow-moving, contextual) and novel (fast-moving, stimulus-driven) components, aligning with the generative structure of language.
The predictive component of Temporal Feature Analysis captures smooth temporal trajectories, event boundaries, and speaker roles in dialogue, while the novel component retains monosemantic features interpretable via standard autointerp pipelines.
In experiments on garden path sentences, stories, and in-context dialogue, Temporal Feature Analysis correctly parses linguistic structure and identifies event boundaries, whereas standard SAEs show significant pitfalls.
The method demonstrates that incorporating data-informed temporal inductive biases is crucial for robust interpretability tools.
papers.limitation: The method assumes that the residual novel component is i.i.d. over time, which may not hold in general.
future_direction: Explore other inductive biases (e.g., hierarchical, compositional) for interpretability.
Apply Temporal Feature Analysis to other modalities (e.g., video, audio).
Conduct more extensive causal intervention studies to validate the interpretability of the novel codes.
papers.abstract: Recovering meaningful concepts from language model activations is a central aim of interpretability. While existing feature extraction methods aim to identify concepts that are independent directions, it is unclear if this assumption can capture the rich temporal structure of language. Specifically, via a Bayesian lens, we demonstrate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) impose priors that assume independence of concepts across time, implying stationarity. Meanwhile, language model representations exhibit rich temporal dynamics, including systematic growth in conceptual dimensionality, context-dependent correlations, and pronounced non-stationarity, in direct conflict with the priors of SAEs. Taking inspiration from computational neuroscience, we introduce a new interpretability objective -- Temporal Feature Analysis -- which possesses a temporal inductive bias to decompose representations at a given time into two parts: a predictable component, which can be inferred from the context, and a residual component, which captures novel information unexplained by the context. Temporal Feature Analyzers correctly parse garden path sentences, identify event boundaries, and more broadly delineate abstract, slow-moving information from novel, fast-moving information, while existing SAEs show significant pitfalls in all the above tasks. Overall, our results underscore the need for inductive biases that match the data in designing robust interpretability tools.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: On the transferability of Sparse Autoencoders for interpreting compressed models
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) trained on uncompressed models be effectively transferred to interpret compressed (pruned) models, and is pruning the original SAE itself a viable alternative to training a new SAE on the pruned model?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs pretrained on uncompressed models can be transferred to pruned models with minimal performance loss, and pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, offering a computationally efficient alternative.
papers.conclusion: Retraining SAEs for each compressed model variant may be unnecessary; pruning the pretrained SAE offers a practical and computationally efficient alternative for post-hoc interpretability analysis of compressed models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model with only slight performance degradation compared to SAEs trained on the compressed model.
Pruning a pretrained SAE (e.g., to 25% sparsity) yields performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, eliminating the need for costly retraining.
The transferability and pruning effectiveness hold across different model architectures (GPT-2 and Gemma-2-2B) and across various interpretability metrics (reconstruction, feature absorption, SCR, TPP, RAVEL).
future_direction: Explore the generalization of these findings to quantized and low-rank compressed models.
Further investigate the role of pruning as an implicit regularizer in interpretability systems.
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs face inference efficiency challenges due to their scale. To address this, many compression methods have been proposed, such as pruning and quantization. However, the effect of compression on a model's interpretability remains elusive. While several model interpretation approaches exist, such as circuit discovery, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have proven particularly effective in decomposing a model's activation space into its feature basis. In this work, we explore the differences in SAEs for the original and compressed models. We find that SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model albeit with slight performance degradation compared to the trained SAE on the compressed model. Furthermore, simply pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model. This finding enables us to mitigate the extensive training costs of SAEs.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
